title: AM-GM for Three Variables from the Cube Factorisation
key_idea: a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc = (a + b + c)((a-b)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (c-a)^2)/2 is a product of non-negative factors
key_idea_summary: The factorisation a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc = (a + b + c)(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - ab - bc - ca) and the identity a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - ab - bc - ca = ((a-b)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (c-a)^2)/2 show the difference is non-negative. Substituting a = x^{1/3} etc. gives AM-GM.

title: AM-GM for Two Numbers from a Single Square
key_idea: the difference of the two sides is half of (sqrt a - sqrt b)^2
key_idea_summary: (a + b)/2 - sqrt(ab) = (sqrt a - sqrt b)^2 / 2 >= 0, with equality iff sqrt a = sqrt b.

title: Archimedes' Arbelos: Its Area Equals the Circle on the Altitude
key_idea: the area of the arbelos is (pi/8)(AB^2 - AC^2 - CB^2) = (pi/4) AC * CB, and CD^2 = AC * CB by the altitude theorem in the right triangle ADB
key_idea_summary: With AC = 2a and CB = 2b, the arbelos has area (pi/2)((a + b)^2 - a^2 - b^2) = pi a b. The triangle ADB is right-angled at D (Thales), so the altitude CD satisfies CD^2 = AC * CB = 4ab, and the circle with diameter CD has area (pi/4) * 4ab = pi ab.

title: A Telescoping Sum of Arctangents
key_idea: 1/(n^2 + n + 1) is the tangent of arctan(n + 1) - arctan(n)
key_idea_summary: By the subtraction formula, tan(arctan(n+1) - arctan n) = ((n+1) - n)/(1 + n(n+1)) = 1/(n^2 + n + 1). So each term is arctan(n+1) - arctan(n), and the partial sums telescope to arctan(N+1), which tends to pi/2.

title: Numbers on a Circle: the Sum of Adjacent Differences Is at Least 2(n - 1)
answer: minimum 2(n - 1), attained by the arrangement 1, 3, 5, ..., (odd numbers up), ..., 6, 4, 2 (even numbers down)
key_idea: the circle contains two paths from 1 to n, and along each path the differences telescope to at least n - 1
key_idea_summary: Going from 1 to n around the circle in either direction, the adjacent differences sum to at least n - 1 by the triangle inequality, and the two directions use disjoint adjacent pairs, so the total is at least 2(n - 1). The arrangement 1, 3, 5, ..., n, ..., 6, 4, 2 attains it.
additional_sources: Fomin, Genkin, Itenberg - Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience)
aliases: sum of absolute differences around a circle
1 to n on a circle minimal total variation
walk from 1 to n and back

title: If x + y + z = 0 Then x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 3xyz
key_idea: the polynomial x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz has the factor x + y + z
key_idea_summary: x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - xy - yz - zx), as expansion verifies. If x + y + z = 0 the right side vanishes. The differences a - b, b - c, c - a sum to zero, so the second identity is a special case.
aliases: cube identity when the sum is zero

title: Which Integers Are Differences of Two Squares
answer: exactly those not congruent to 2 mod 4 (odd numbers and multiples of 4)
key_idea: x^2 - y^2 = (x - y)(x + y), and the two factors have the same parity
key_idea_summary: Factor n = (x - y)(x + y). The factors x - y and x + y have the same parity, so n is odd or divisible by 4. Conversely, an odd n = 1 * n gives x = (n+1)/2, y = (n-1)/2, and n = 4m = 2 * 2m gives x = m + 1, y = m - 1.
aliases: numbers 2 mod 4 are not differences of squares

title: F_1 + F_2 + ... + F_n = F_{n+2} - 1
key_idea: write each term as a difference: F_k = F_{k+2} - F_{k+1}
key_idea_summary: The recursion F_{k+2} = F_{k+1} + F_k says F_k = F_{k+2} - F_{k+1}. Summing from k = 1 to n telescopes: (F_3 - F_2) + (F_4 - F_3) + ... + (F_{n+2} - F_{n+1}) = F_{n+2} - F_2 = F_{n+2} - 1.

title: A Degree-d Polynomial Has Constant d-th Differences
key_idea: the difference of the leading term (n + 1)^d - n^d has leading term d n^{d-1} by the binomial theorem, and lower terms only produce lower degrees
key_idea_summary: For p = a_d n^d + lower terms, (n + 1)^d - n^d = d n^{d-1} + lower terms by the binomial theorem, and differences of lower-degree terms have even lower degree. So Delta p = d a_d n^{d-1} + lower terms. Iterating, Delta^d p = d! a_d, a constant, and Delta^{d+1} p = 0. Consequently a sequence whose d-th differences are constant is given by a polynomial of degree d.
aliases: d-th difference equals d! times the leading coefficient

title: The Product of Four Consecutive Integers Plus One Is a Perfect Square
key_idea: pair the outer and inner factors: n(n + 3) = m - 1 and (n + 1)(n + 2) = m + 1 with m = n^2 + 3n + 1, so the product is m^2 - 1
key_idea_summary: Group the factors as [n(n + 3)] [(n + 1)(n + 2)] = (n^2 + 3n)(n^2 + 3n + 2). With m = n^2 + 3n + 1 these are (m - 1)(m + 1) = m^2 - 1, so the product plus one is m^2.

title: Summing a Geometric Series by Shifting
key_idea: multiply the sum by r and subtract: almost everything cancels
key_idea_summary: rS = r + r^2 + ... + r^{n+1}. Subtracting S from rS cancels all the middle terms, leaving rS - S = r^{n+1} - 1.

title: The Harmonic Series Diverges (Oresme's Grouping)
key_idea: group the terms into blocks 1/3 + 1/4, 1/5 + ... + 1/8, ...; each block exceeds 1/2
key_idea_summary: The block of terms 1/(2^k + 1) through 1/2^{k+1} has 2^k terms each at least 1/2^{k+1}, so it sums to at least 1/2. Infinitely many blocks each contribute at least 1/2, so the partial sums exceed every bound.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Among Rectangles of Given Perimeter the Square Has the Largest Area
key_idea: write the sides as s/2 + t and s/2 - t; the area is (s/2)^2 - t^2
key_idea_summary: Sides a + b = s can be written as s/2 + t and s/2 - t. The area (s/2 + t)(s/2 - t) = (s/2)^2 - t^2 is largest when t = 0, i.e. for the square.
aliases: maximum area rectangle with fixed perimeter

title: If 2^n - 1 Is Prime Then n Is Prime; If 2^n + 1 Is Prime Then n Is a Power of 2
key_idea: x^{ab} - 1 has the factor x^a - 1, and x^{ab} + 1 has the factor x^a + 1 when b is odd
key_idea_summary: If n = ab with 1 < a < n then 2^a - 1 is a proper divisor of 2^n - 1 by the geometric series identity, so 2^n - 1 is composite. If n has an odd factor b > 1, n = ab, then 2^a + 1 divides 2^n + 1 = (2^a)^b + 1, again giving a proper factor.
aliases: Fermat prime exponent is a power of two

title: Every Odd Square Is 1 Modulo 8
key_idea: (2k + 1)^2 - 1 = 4k(k + 1), and k(k + 1) is even as a product of consecutive integers
key_idea_summary: (2k + 1)^2 = 4k(k + 1) + 1, and one of k, k + 1 is even, so 8 divides 4k(k + 1) and the square is 1 mod 8. Even squares are 0 or 4 mod 8, so squares are 0, 1, 4 mod 8; sums of two squares avoid 3, 6, 7 mod 8, and sums of three avoid 7.
additional_sources: Niven, Zuckerman, Montgomery - An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers

title: Sum of 1/(k sqrt k) Converges, by Comparison with a Telescoping Series
answer: proved (the partial sums are bounded by 3)
key_idea: bound each term 1/k^{3/2} by a difference 2(1/sqrt(k - 1) - 1/sqrt k), which telescopes
key_idea_summary: For k >= 2, 1/(k sqrt k) < 2/(sqrt(k-1) sqrt k (sqrt(k-1) + sqrt k)) = 2(1/sqrt(k-1) - 1/sqrt k). Summing from 2 to n telescopes to 2(1 - 1/sqrt n) < 2, so the whole sum is less than 1 + 2 = 3.

title: a - b Divides P(a) - P(b) for Integer Polynomials
key_idea: each monomial difference a^k - b^k has the factor a - b
key_idea_summary: P(a) - P(b) is a sum of terms c_k (a^k - b^k), and a^k - b^k = (a - b)(a^{k-1} + ... + b^{k-1}). Hence a - b divides P(a) - P(b). For the application, 3 - 1 = 2 would have to divide 5 - 2 = 3.
aliases: P(a) - P(b) divisible by a - b
no integer polynomial with P(1)=2 and P(3)=5

title: A Prime p Divides C(p, k) for 0 < k < p
key_idea: in k! C(p, k) = p (p - 1) ... (p - k + 1) the prime p divides the right side but not k!
key_idea_summary: The identity C(p, k) = p(p - 1)...(p - k + 1)/k! shows that k! C(p, k) is divisible by p. Since k < p, none of the factors of k! is divisible by p, so p does not divide k!, and as p is prime it must divide C(p, k). Expanding (a + b)^p, all the middle binomial terms vanish mod p.

title: The Quadratic Mean Exceeds the Arithmetic Mean
key_idea: n sum x_i^2 - (sum x_i)^2 = sum over pairs of (x_i - x_j)^2, a sum of squares
key_idea_summary: Expanding, n sum x_i^2 - (sum x_i)^2 = sum over i < j of (x_i - x_j)^2 >= 0. Dividing by n^2 and taking square roots gives QM >= AM, with equality iff all x_i are equal.
aliases: sum of squares at least square of sum over n

title: A Repunit with a Composite Number of Digits Is Composite
key_idea: R_{ab} = R_a * (1 + 10^a + 10^{2a} + ... + 10^{(b-1)a}): a repunit with ab digits splits into b blocks of a ones
key_idea_summary: Write the ab ones as b blocks of a ones. Then R_{ab} = R_a (1 + 10^a + ... + 10^{(b-1)a}), a proper factorisation when a, b > 1. So a prime repunit has a prime number of digits (the converse fails: R_3 = 111 = 3 * 37).
aliases: 111...1 prime implies number of digits prime

title: A Rope Around the Earth Lengthened by One Metre
answer: about 16 cm (1/(2 pi) metres), independent of the planet's radius
key_idea: circumference is a linear function of the radius, so a fixed change in circumference gives a fixed change in radius
key_idea_summary: C = 2 pi r, so a change of 1 m in C changes r by 1/(2 pi) m, about 16 cm, no matter what r was. The Earth's size cancels completely.
additional_sources: Gardner - The Colossal Book of Short Puzzles and Problems
aliases: circumference and radius are linearly related

title: 6 Divides n^3 - n, and 30 Divides n^5 - n
key_idea: n^3 - n = (n - 1) n (n + 1) is a product of three consecutive integers, one divisible by 2 and one by 3
key_idea_summary: n^3 - n = (n - 1)n(n + 1). Among three consecutive integers one is a multiple of 3 and at least one is even, so the product is divisible by 6. For n^5 - n = (n - 1)n(n + 1)(n^2 + 1), the factor 5 comes from Fermat's little theorem or from checking n mod 5.

title: n^4 + 4 Is Never Prime for n > 1 (Sophie Germain's Identity)
key_idea: complete the square: n^4 + 4 = (n^2 + 2)^2 - (2n)^2, a difference of two squares
key_idea_summary: n^4 + 4 = (n^2 + 2)^2 - 4n^2 = (n^2 - 2n + 2)(n^2 + 2n + 2). For n > 1 both factors exceed 1, so the number is composite.

title: The St. Petersburg Game Has Infinite Expected Value
answer: infinite: each term of the expectation sum equals 1
key_idea: the probability of stopping at toss k is 2^{-k}, exactly cancelling the payout 2^k, so every term of the expectation is 1 and there are infinitely many terms
key_idea_summary: P(first head at toss k) = 2^{-k} and the payout is 2^k, so the k-th contribution to the expectation is 2^k * 2^{-k} = 1. The expectation is 1 + 1 + 1 + ..., which diverges.
additional_sources: Feller - An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, vol. 1

title: 1*1! + 2*2! + ... + n*n! = (n+1)! - 1
aliases: sum of k times k factorial

title: Summing n/2^n by the Shift Trick
key_idea: subtract S/2 from S: the difference is a plain geometric series
key_idea_summary: S/2 = 1/4 + 2/8 + 3/16 + .... Subtracting term by term, S - S/2 = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... = 1, since the coefficients n - (n - 1) = 1. So S/2 = 1 and S = 2.

title: The Sum of Squares Formula from Telescoping Cubes
key_idea: sum the identity (k + 1)^3 - k^3 = 3k^2 + 3k + 1 over k; the left side telescopes to (n + 1)^3 - 1
key_idea_summary: Summing (k + 1)^3 - k^3 = 3k^2 + 3k + 1 from k = 1 to n gives (n + 1)^3 - 1 = 3 S_2 + 3 S_1 + n, where S_1 = n(n+1)/2 is known. Solving for S_2 yields the formula.

title: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 >= xy + yz + zx as a Sum of Squares
key_idea: twice the difference is a sum of three squares
key_idea_summary: 2(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - xy - yz - zx) = (x-y)^2 + (y-z)^2 + (z-x)^2, which is non-negative and vanishes only when x = y = z.
aliases: a^2 + b^2 + c^2 >= ab + bc + ca

title: The Product of (1 - 1/k^2) Telescopes
key_idea: factor each term as ((k - 1)/k)((k + 1)/k) and let the two chains cancel
key_idea_summary: 1 - 1/k^2 = (k - 1)(k + 1)/k^2. The product of (k - 1)/k over k = 2..n is 1/n and the product of (k + 1)/k is (n + 1)/2. Multiplying gives (n + 1)/(2n).

title: Summing 1/(k(k+1)) by Telescoping
answer: n/(n+1); the infinite series sums to 1
key_idea: write each term as a difference of consecutive quantities
key_idea_summary: 1/(k(k+1)) = 1/k - 1/(k+1). Summing, every intermediate term cancels with its neighbour, leaving 1 - 1/(n+1).

title: Titu's Lemma (the Engel Form of Cauchy-Schwarz)
key_idea: apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the vectors (a_i/sqrt(b_i)) and (sqrt(b_i))
key_idea_summary: Cauchy-Schwarz gives (sum of (a_i/sqrt b_i) sqrt b_i)^2 <= (sum a_i^2/b_i)(sum b_i). The left side is (sum a_i)^2, and dividing by sum b_i gives the lemma.

title: Fixed Perimeter, Maximal Area: the Equilateral Triangle (Heron plus AM-GM)
key_idea: Heron's formula makes the area a product s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c) with (s - a) + (s - b) + (s - c) = s fixed, and AM-GM maximises a product with fixed sum when the factors are equal
key_idea_summary: By Heron, area^2 = s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c). The three factors s - a, s - b, s - c are positive and sum to 3s - 2s = s, so by AM-GM their product is at most (s/3)^3, with equality iff s - a = s - b = s - c, i.e. a = b = c.

title: For Composite n > 4, n Divides (n - 1)!
key_idea: a composite n = ab with 1 < a < b < n has both factors among 1..n-1; if n = p^2 then p and 2p both appear once p > 2
key_idea_summary: If n = ab with a != b, both a and b are distinct numbers below n, so their product n divides (n - 1)!. If n = p^2 with p > 2, then p and 2p are distinct numbers below n = p^2 (since 2p < p^2 for p > 2), and their product 2p^2 is divisible by n. Only n = 4 escapes: 3! = 6 = 2 mod 4.

title: Achilles and the Tortoise: an Infinite Series with a Finite Sum
answer: Achilles catches the tortoise after 100 + 10 + 1 + ... = 111.11 metres
key_idea: the infinitely many stages have distances (and times) forming a geometric series with a finite sum
key_idea_summary: The stages have lengths 100, 10, 1, 0.1, ..., which sum to 100/(1 - 1/10) = 1000/9 metres, and the corresponding times likewise form a convergent geometric series. Infinitely many stages fit into a finite distance and a finite time, so the argument only shows that Achilles has not caught up before that moment.
aliases: infinitely many steps in finite time

title: Solid Dominoes Cannot Fill a 3x3x3 Cube with the Centre Removed
key_idea: colour the cubes in a three-dimensional checkerboard; the corners' colour has 14 cells and the other 13, and the centre is of the minority colour
key_idea_summary: Colour cell (x, y, z) by the parity of x + y + z. The 3x3x3 cube has 14 cells of the corners' colour and 13 of the other; the centre is of the minority colour, so removing it leaves 14 and 12. Every domino covers one cell of each colour, so 13 dominoes would cover 13 and 13.

title: Walking on the Edges of a Cube
key_idea: colour the vertices by the parity of their coordinate sum
key_idea_summary: Place the cube at {0,1}^3 and colour a vertex by the parity of x + y + z. Each edge joins vertices of opposite colour, so the colour alternates with every step; returning to the start needs an even number of steps.
additional_sources: Fomin, Genkin, Itenberg - Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience)
aliases: bug on a cube returns after even steps

title: 100 Grasshoppers on a Triangular Board
answer: proved (at least 10 empty cells after any odd number of hops)
key_idea: two-colour the cells; hops always change colour
key_idea_summary: Colour upward-pointing cells red and downward-pointing ones brown; every hop goes from one colour to the other. There are 55 red and 45 brown cells, so after an odd number of hops all grasshoppers that started red are on brown cells and vice versa: at most 45 red cells are occupied, leaving at least 10 empty.

title: A Knight Returns to Its Square Only after an Even Number of Moves
key_idea: every knight move changes the colour of the square
key_idea_summary: A knight moves from a square to one of the opposite colour. After k moves it is on the starting colour iff k is even. A closed tour of an n-square board returns after n moves, so n must be even.
aliases: knight cannot return in odd moves
no closed knight's tour on odd boards

title: 25 Knights on a 5x5 Board Cannot All Move at Once
key_idea: a knight move changes the colour of its square, and the 5x5 board has 13 squares of one colour and 12 of the other
key_idea_summary: Every knight moves to a square of the opposite colour. If all knights moved simultaneously onto distinct squares, the 13 knights on black squares would need 13 distinct white squares, but there are only 12.
additional_sources: Fomin, Genkin, Itenberg - Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience)
aliases: knights on a 5x5 board simultaneous move

title: No Closed Knight's Tour on a 4 x n Board
key_idea: compare two colourings, one of which the knight is forced to alternate
key_idea_summary: Colour the two outer rows "outer" and the two inner rows "inner". From an outer square a knight must land on an inner square. In a closed tour with equally many outer and inner squares, the tour must therefore alternate outer/inner. It also alternates black/white. Two alternating patterns of the same period coincide or are complementary, so all outer squares would be one chessboard colour, which is false.
aliases: closed knight's tour on four rows

title: Mutilated Checkerboard
key_idea: checkerboard coloring
key_idea_summary: Every domino covers exactly one black and one white square, so any tiled region has equally many squares of each color. Two diagonally opposite corners have the same color, so the mutilated board does not.
aliases: domino tiling of a board with two opposite corners removed

title: A Rectangle Tiled by Rectangles with an Integer Side Has an Integer Side
key_idea: colour the plane as a checkerboard of 1/2 x 1/2 squares; every tile with an integer side is colour-balanced
key_idea_summary: Colour the plane in a checkerboard pattern with squares of side 1/2, corner at the big rectangle's corner. Any rectangle with an integer side, however placed, contains equal black and white area. So the big rectangle is balanced, and a rectangle with corner at the origin is balanced only if one of its sides is an integer.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK
additional_sources: S. Wagon, Fourteen Proofs of a Result About Tiling a Rectangle

title: A 10x10 Board Cannot Be Tiled by 1x4 Tiles
key_idea: colour diagonally with four colours
key_idea_summary: Give the cell (i, j) colour (i + j) mod 4. Every 1x4 tile, horizontal or vertical, covers one cell of each colour. But the 10x10 board has 25, 26, 25, 24 cells of the four colours, so no tiling exists.
aliases: straight tetromino tiling of a 10x10 board

title: Which Square Can Be Removed So Straight Trominoes Tile the 8x8 Board?
answer: only the four squares (3,3), (3,6), (6,3), (6,6) (rows and columns numbered 1 to 8)
key_idea: two diagonal three-colourings force the removed square to lie in the least-used colour class of both
key_idea_summary: Colour cell (i, j) with (i + j) mod 3. Every straight tromino covers one cell of each colour, and the colour counts are 21, 21, 22. So the removed cell must have the colour with 22 cells. Colouring by (i - j) mod 3 gives a second condition. Only four cells satisfy both, and for those explicit tilings exist.
aliases: straight tromino tiling of a deficient chessboard

title: A 10x10 Board Cannot Be Tiled by T-Tetrominoes
key_idea: on a chessboard colouring every T covers 3 + 1 squares of the two colours
key_idea_summary: A T-tetromino always covers three squares of one colour and one of the other. If a tiles cover 3 black + 1 white and b tiles cover 1 black + 3 white, then a + b = 25 and 3a + b = 50 (black squares), giving 2a = 25, impossible.
aliases: T-shaped tiles on a square board

title: Horizontal and Vertical Dominoes Come in Even Numbers
key_idea: color the board in vertical stripes
key_idea_summary: Color the columns alternately black and white. A horizontal domino covers one square of each colour; a vertical domino covers two squares of the same colour. The 32 black squares are covered by all H horizontal dominoes plus pairs from vertical ones, so H is even.
aliases: number of horizontal dominoes in a tiling is even

title: The Art Gallery Theorem (Fisk's Three-Colouring Proof)
answer: proved (floor(n/3) guards always suffice, and are sometimes necessary)
key_idea: triangulate, three-colour the vertices, and post guards on the least-used colour
key_idea_summary: Triangulate the polygon with diagonals. The vertices of a triangulated polygon can be coloured with three colours so that every triangle has all three colours. Some colour is used at most n/3 times; a guard at each vertex of that colour sees every triangle, hence the whole museum.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Bertrand's Ballot Theorem by the Reflection Principle
key_idea: reflect the initial segment of a bad path across the axis
key_idea_summary: Draw the count as a path of +1 (A) and -1 (B) steps. Bad paths are those touching 0 after the start. Bad paths starting with A biject with paths starting with B (reflect the part up to the first return to 0), and every path starting with B is bad. So the number of good paths is (paths starting with A) - (paths starting with B).
additional_sources: Feller - An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, vol. 1

title: Bertrand's Box Paradox
key_idea: count coins, not boxes: three gold coins are equally likely to be the one drawn, and two of them have a gold partner
key_idea_summary: Drawing a random box then a random coin is the same as drawing one of the six coins uniformly. Given the coin is gold, it is one of the three gold coins with equal probability; two of those three share their box with another gold coin. So the probability is 2/3.

title: Every Graph Has a Bipartite Subgraph with at Least Half the Edges
key_idea: put each vertex on a random side; each edge crosses with probability 1/2
key_idea_summary: Assign each vertex independently to side A or B with a fair coin. Each edge has its endpoints on different sides with probability 1/2, so the expected number of crossing edges is m/2. Some outcome must achieve at least the expectation.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK
aliases: random cut has half the edges in expectation

title: The Birthday Paradox via the Complement
key_idea: compute the probability that all birthdays are different, a product of shrinking factors, and subtract from 1
key_idea_summary: The chance that n people all have distinct birthdays is (364/365)(363/365)...((366 - n)/365). Multiplying these factors, the product drops below 1/2 at n = 23. The 'paradox' dissolves on noticing there are C(23,2) = 253 pairs, each a potential match.

title: Buffon's Needle via Linearity of Expectation (Barbier's Argument)
key_idea: the expected number of crossings is additive in length, so compute it for a circle
key_idea_summary: For a needle of length L <= d, the probability of crossing equals the expected number of crossings E(L). Bending or chaining needles does not change the expectation of the total (linearity), so E is proportional to length: E(L) = cL. A circle of diameter d, a "noodle" of length pi d, crosses the lines exactly twice always, so c * pi d = 2.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Counting Necklaces with Burnside's Lemma
key_idea: count pairs (rotation, colouring fixed by it): the identity fixes all a^p colourings and each of the p - 1 nontrivial rotations fixes only the a constant colourings; orbits = fixed points averaged over the group
key_idea_summary: Burnside's lemma says the number of orbits equals the average number of colourings fixed by a group element. The identity rotation fixes a^p colourings. A rotation by k != 0 positions, p prime, has a single cycle, so it fixes only the a monochromatic colourings. Hence the number of necklaces is (a^p + (p - 1)a)/p.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Cantor-Schroder-Bernstein: Injections Both Ways Give a Bijection
key_idea: follow each element backwards through f and g as far as possible; the chains starting in A are matched by f, the chains starting in B by g, and the two-way infinite chains by either
key_idea_summary: Trace each element backwards through f and g; by injectivity the chain of predecessors is unique and either stops in A, stops in B, or never stops. Use f on elements of A whose chain stops in A or never stops, and g^{-1} on those whose chain stops in B. Within each chain, an alternating sequence of A- and B-elements, the chosen map pairs the elements off perfectly.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK
aliases: injections both ways imply equal cardinality

title: An Independent Set of Size at Least Sum 1/(d(v) + 1) (Caro-Wei)
key_idea: order the vertices randomly and select those that come before all their neighbours; a vertex is selected with probability 1/(d(v) + 1)
key_idea_summary: Choose a uniformly random ordering of the vertices and let S be the set of vertices preceding all their neighbours. S is independent (of two adjacent vertices, only the earlier one can be in S). Vertex v is first among itself and its d(v) neighbours with probability 1/(d(v) + 1), so E|S| = sum of 1/(d(v) + 1), and some ordering achieves at least that. Convexity of 1/(x + 1) then gives n/(d + 1).

title: Counting Balanced Parentheses by Reflecting Bad Paths
answer: the Catalan number C(2n, n)/(n + 1) = C(2n, n) - C(2n, n + 1)
key_idea: reflect the part of a bad path after its first dip below zero; bad paths correspond to paths ending at level -2
key_idea_summary: Among all C(2n, n) paths with n ups and n downs, the bad ones touch level -1. Reflect the portion after the first visit to -1 (swap ups and downs): the result ends at -2 and has n - 1 ups and n + 1 downs. This is a bijection between bad paths and all paths to -2, of which there are C(2n, n + 1). So the good paths number C(2n, n) - C(2n, n + 1).

title: Cayley's Formula via Prufer Codes
key_idea: repeatedly remove the smallest leaf and record its neighbour; the recorded sequence of length n - 2 is a bijective code
key_idea_summary: Delete the leaf with the smallest label and write down its neighbour; repeat until two vertices remain. This gives a sequence of n - 2 labels. The process is reversible (the leaves are exactly the labels not yet in the remaining code), so trees correspond bijectively to sequences in {1..n}^{n-2}.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: The Chinese Remainder Theorem by Counting
key_idea: the map x -> (x mod m, x mod n) from Z/mn to Z/m x Z/n is injective, and both sets have mn elements, so it is a bijection
key_idea_summary: If x and y in {0, ..., mn - 1} have the same residues mod m and mod n, then both m and n divide x - y, and since they are coprime mn divides x - y, so x = y. An injective map between finite sets of equal size mn is surjective, so every pair (a, b) is hit exactly once.

title: Three Consecutive Numbers on a Circle Sum to at Least 17
key_idea: add up all ten consecutive triples: each number is counted three times
key_idea_summary: The ten triple-sums add up to 3 * (1 + ... + 10) = 165, so their average is 16.5, and some triple sum is at least 17.
additional_sources: Fomin, Genkin, Itenberg - Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience)
aliases: 1 to 10 on a circle three consecutive

title: Sum of k C(n, k) by Choosing a Chair
key_idea: count committees with a designated chair in two ways
key_idea_summary: A committee of size k with a chair can be formed by choosing the committee (C(n,k) ways) then the chair (k ways), or by choosing the chair first (n ways) and then any subset of the other n - 1 people (2^{n-1} ways).

title: A Countable Union of Countable Sets Is Countable
key_idea: arrange the elements in an infinite grid, a_{ij} = the j-th element of A_i, and walk the grid along successive anti-diagonals
key_idea_summary: List each A_i as a_{i1}, a_{i2}, .... The elements form an infinite table indexed by pairs (i, j), and the pairs can be enumerated by anti-diagonals: (1,1), then (1,2), (2,1), then (1,3), (2,2), (3,1), and so on, since each anti-diagonal i + j = s is finite. This lists every element of the union (skipping repeats), so the union is countable.

title: Non-Crossing Diagonals in a Convex Polygon Always Number n - 3
answer: proved (always n - 3 diagonals and n - 2 triangles)
key_idea: count the angle sum of the resulting triangles in two ways
key_idea_summary: The diagonals cut the polygon into T triangles with total angle sum 180 T degrees; these angles exactly fill the polygon's angles, which sum to 180(n - 2). So T = n - 2. Counting triangle sides, 3T = n + 2D (each diagonal is a side of two triangles), giving D = n - 3.
aliases: triangulation of a convex polygon has n - 2 triangles

title: The Coupon Collector Needs about n log n Draws
answer: n (1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n) = n H_n, about n ln n
key_idea: split the process into stages: while k types are held, each box is new with probability (n - k)/n, so the k-th stage takes n/(n - k) boxes on average
key_idea_summary: The waiting time for the (k+1)-st new type, given k types already, is geometric with success probability (n - k)/n, so its mean is n/(n - k). Summing over k = 0..n-1 by linearity gives n (1/n + 1/(n-1) + ... + 1) = n H_n.
additional_sources: Feller - An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, vol. 1
aliases: expected draws to collect all n coupons

title: Derangements and the Hat-Check Problem
answer: D(n) = n! sum over k of (-1)^k / k!, probability tending to 1/e
key_idea: count the complement with inclusion-exclusion over the set of people who do get their own hat
key_idea_summary: Let A_i be the set of orders in which person i gets their hat. The number of orders avoiding all A_i is, by inclusion-exclusion, sum over k of (-1)^k C(n,k) (n-k)!, since any k specified people getting their hats leaves (n-k)! orders. Simplifying gives n! times the partial sum of the series for e^{-1}.
aliases: probability that no one gets their own hat

title: Interior Intersection Points of the Diagonals of a Convex n-gon
key_idea: a crossing is determined by, and determines, four vertices
key_idea_summary: Any four vertices of a convex polygon form a convex quadrilateral whose two diagonals cross at exactly one interior point; conversely a crossing of two diagonals has four distinct endpoints. So crossings correspond bijectively to 4-element subsets of the vertices.
aliases: number of diagonal crossings in a convex polygon

title: A Convex n-gon Has n(n - 3)/2 Diagonals
key_idea: each vertex is an endpoint of n - 3 diagonals, and each diagonal has two endpoints
key_idea_summary: From each of the n vertices, n - 3 diagonals leave (to all vertices except itself and its two neighbours). Counting endpoints, n(n - 3) counts every diagonal exactly twice, so there are n(n - 3)/2 diagonals. Equivalently: C(n, 2) segments between vertices minus the n sides.
aliases: number of diagonals of a polygon

title: Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem
key_idea: the N + 1 fractional parts {0}, {alpha}, ..., {N alpha} fall into N intervals of length 1/N
key_idea_summary: Two of the N + 1 numbers {k alpha}, 0 <= k <= N, lie in the same interval [j/N, (j+1)/N). Their difference is (k_2 - k_1) alpha minus an integer, of absolute value less than 1/N, with 1 <= k_2 - k_1 <= N.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: The Number and Sum of Divisors from Prime Exponents
key_idea: a divisor is the same thing as a choice of an exponent 0..e_i for each prime, and expanding the product of geometric sums lists every divisor once
key_idea_summary: By unique factorisation, d divides n iff d = p_1^{a_1} ... p_k^{a_k} with 0 <= a_i <= e_i. The choices are independent, giving (e_1 + 1)...(e_k + 1) divisors. Expanding the product (1 + p_1 + ... + p_1^{e_1}) ... (1 + p_k + ... + p_k^{e_k}) produces exactly one term per divisor, namely the divisor itself, so the product is the sum of divisors.

title: Erdos-Ko-Rado via Katona's Circle Argument
answer: proved (attained by all k-sets containing a fixed element)
key_idea: arrange the n elements on a circle; among the n arcs of length k at most k belong to the family; average over all circular arrangements
key_idea_summary: Arrange the n elements on a circle and look at the n arcs of k consecutive elements. Pairwise intersecting arcs number at most k. Counting pairs (cyclic arrangement, arc belonging to F) in two ways, each of the (n-1)! arrangements contributes at most k while each member of F is an arc in k!(n-k)! arrangements, so |F| k! (n-k)! <= k (n-1)!, i.e. |F| <= C(n-1, k-1).
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Erdos-Szekeres, Every Sequence of mn + 1 Numbers Has a Monotone Subsequence
key_idea: label each term by the lengths of the longest increasing and decreasing subsequences ending there; labels are distinct
key_idea_summary: Give term x the pair (i, d): the length of the longest increasing and the longest decreasing subsequence ending at x. For two terms x before y, either y > x (then y's i is larger) or y < x (then y's d is larger), so all mn + 1 pairs are distinct. If all i <= m and all d <= n there are only mn possible pairs: contradiction.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Euclid's Construction of Even Perfect Numbers
key_idea: the divisors of N are 2^i and 2^i q (q = 2^p - 1 prime), two geometric progressions whose sums are easy
key_idea_summary: With q = 2^p - 1 prime, the divisors of N = 2^{p-1} q are 2^i for 0 <= i <= p - 1 and 2^i q for the same i. Their total is (1 + 2 + ... + 2^{p-1})(1 + q) = (2^p - 1) 2^p = 2N. A number whose divisors sum to twice itself is perfect.

title: Euler's Totient Formula by Inclusion-Exclusion
key_idea: count the integers divisible by at least one prime factor of n by inclusion-exclusion; multiples of a set of primes are counted exactly by n divided by their product
key_idea_summary: An integer in 1..n is not coprime to n iff it is divisible by some prime p dividing n. The number of multiples of p_1 ... p_k (distinct prime factors of n) in 1..n is exactly n/(p_1 ... p_k). Inclusion-exclusion gives phi(n) = n - sum n/p + sum n/(pq) - ... = n product (1 - 1/p).

title: As Many Even-Sized Subsets as Odd-Sized Subsets
key_idea: toggle a fixed element in or out
key_idea_summary: Fix one element x. Mapping a subset S to S with x added (if absent) or removed (if present) changes the size by one, so it pairs each even subset with an odd subset and is its own inverse.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK
aliases: alternating sum of binomial coefficients is zero

title: A Random Permutation Has about ln n Cycles on Average
key_idea: build the permutation by inserting elements one at a time into the cycle structure; element k starts a new cycle with probability 1/k
key_idea_summary: Insert the elements 1, 2, ..., n one after another, each element either opening a new cycle or being placed after one of the k - 1 earlier elements in its cycle; all k choices are equally likely and this produces a uniform permutation. Element k starts a new cycle with probability 1/k, so by linearity the expected number of cycles is sum of 1/k = H_n.

title: The Expected Number of Runs in n Coin Tosses
key_idea: a new run starts at position k > 1 exactly when toss k differs from toss k - 1, which has probability 1/2
key_idea_summary: The number of runs is 1 plus the number of positions k = 2..n at which the outcome changes. Each change happens with probability 1/2, so by linearity the expectation is 1 + (n - 1)/2 = (n + 1)/2.
additional_sources: Feller - An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, vol. 1
aliases: indicator for a change of symbol

title: Some Element Is at Least the Average
answer: proved; some student solved at least ceiling(100/26) = 4 problems
key_idea: if every number were below the average, the sum would be below n times the average
key_idea_summary: If all x_i were less than A, then the sum of the x_i would be less than nA, contradicting the definition of A. So the maximum is at least the average, and for integers at least the ceiling of the average. With 100 problems among 26 students the average is 3.85, so someone solved at least 4.
aliases: maximum is at least the mean

title: Fermat's Little Theorem by Multiplying All Residues by a

key_idea_summary: The numbers a, 2a, ..., (p-1)a are pairwise incongruent mod p (a difference ka - ja = (k - j)a is not divisible by p) and none is 0, so they are the nonzero residues in some order. Multiplying them, a^{p-1}(p-1)! = (p-1)! mod p, and cancelling (p-1)!, which is coprime to p, gives a^{p-1} = 1.
aliases: Fermat's little theorem via permutation of residues

title: Among 55 Numbers from 1 to 100, Two Differ by Exactly 10
key_idea: split into blocks of 20, each of which is 10 pairs {k, k+10}
key_idea_summary: The five blocks 1-20, 21-40, ..., 81-100 each consist of ten pairs {k, k + 10}. Some block contains at least 11 chosen numbers, so two of them lie in the same pair.
additional_sources: Fomin, Genkin, Itenberg - Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience)

title: Among 52 Integers, Two Have Sum or Difference Divisible by 100
key_idea: group residues mod 100 into the 51 boxes {r, 100 - r}
key_idea_summary: The boxes {0}, {50}, {1,99}, {2,98}, ..., {49,51} number 51. Two of 52 integers have residues in the same box; if the residues are equal the difference is divisible by 100, if they are r and 100 - r the sum is.
additional_sources: Fomin, Genkin, Itenberg - Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience)

title: The Fisher-Yates Shuffle Produces Every Permutation Equally Often
key_idea: the random choices (j_n, j_{n-1}, ..., j_2) range over n * (n - 1) * ... * 2 = n! equally likely sequences, and different sequences give different permutations
key_idea_summary: There are n! sequences of choices, each with probability 1/n!. The map from choice sequences to output permutations is injective: the first choice determines which element ends in the last position, the next choice which element ends in the second-last position, and so on, so the output determines the choices. An injective map between two sets of size n! is a bijection, so each permutation has probability exactly 1/n!.
additional_sources: Knuth - The Art of Computer Programming, vol. 2

title: Among Five Lattice Points, Two Have a Lattice Midpoint
key_idea: classify points by the parities of their coordinates
key_idea_summary: There are only four parity classes (even/odd, even/odd). Two of five points share a class, and then both coordinate sums are even, so the midpoint is a lattice point.

title: Why There Are Exactly Five Platonic Solids
key_idea: count edges from faces and from vertices, plug into Euler's formula, and get 1/p + 1/q > 1/2
key_idea_summary: Each face has p edges and each edge lies in 2 faces, so pF = 2E; each vertex has q edges and each edge has 2 ends, so qV = 2E. Euler gives 2E/q - E + 2E/p = 2, so 1/p + 1/q = 1/2 + 1/E > 1/2. With p, q >= 3 only five pairs satisfy this.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Five Points on a Sphere, Four in a Closed Hemisphere
key_idea: take the great circle through two of the points; the other three split between the two hemispheres it bounds
key_idea_summary: Any two of the points lie on a great circle, which bounds two closed hemispheres, both containing those two points. The remaining three points are divided between the hemispheres, so one hemisphere gets at least two of them, hence at least four points in total.
aliases: four of five points in a hemisphere

title: Five Points in a Unit Square, Two Are Close

key_idea_summary: Divide the square into four squares of side 1/2. Five points in four squares put two points in the same quarter, whose diameter (its diagonal) is sqrt(2)/2.
aliases: partition the square into four quarters

title: At Most 14 Non-Attacking Bishops on a Chessboard
key_idea: there are 15 diagonals in one direction, but the two single-square end diagonals lie on the same diagonal of the other direction
key_idea_summary: Bishops must occupy distinct diagonals of one direction, of which there are 15. The two corner squares a1 and h8 are each a whole diagonal of that direction, yet they lie on the same long diagonal of the other direction, so at most one of them can be used: at most 14 bishops. Fourteen are easily placed (e.g. eight on the first row and six on the last row, avoiding the corners on the last row).

title: The Friendship Paradox: Your Friends Have More Friends than You
key_idea: averaging over friendships weights each person by their degree, and the degree-weighted average of degrees is at least the plain average (Cauchy-Schwarz)
key_idea_summary: Pick a random person, then a random friend of theirs; the friend is chosen with probability proportional to their degree. The expected degree of a degree-weighted random vertex is (sum of d^2)/(sum of d), and by Cauchy-Schwarz (sum of d^2)/(sum of d) >= (sum of d)/n, the ordinary average degree.
additional_sources: S. Feld - Why your friends have more friends than you do

title: A Regular Bipartite Graph Has a Perfect Matching
key_idea: count the edges leaving a subset S of one side: k|S| edges land on the neighbourhood N(S), which absorbs at most k|N(S)| edges, so |N(S)| >= |S|
key_idea_summary: For a subset S of the left side, the k|S| edges out of S all end in N(S). Each vertex of N(S) has degree k, so N(S) can receive at most k|N(S)| edges. Hence k|S| <= k|N(S)|, i.e. |N(S)| >= |S|: Hall's condition holds, and a perfect matching exists (both sides have the same size by the same count applied to S = A).
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK
aliases: Konig's theorem on regular bipartite graphs

title: The Number of People Who Shook Hands an Odd Number of Times Is Even
key_idea: count handshake-ends two ways
key_idea_summary: Each handshake has two ends, so the sum over people of their handshake counts is twice the number of handshakes, an even number. An even sum must contain an even number of odd terms.

title: Hilbert's Hotel Accommodates Infinitely Many New Guests

key_idea: an infinite set is in bijection with a proper subset of itself
key_idea_summary: Sending the guest in room n to room n + 1 frees room 1. Sending the guest in room n to room 2n frees all odd-numbered rooms, infinitely many, for the newcomers.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: The Hockey-Stick Identity by the Largest Element
key_idea: classify (r+1)-subsets of {1, ..., n+1} by their largest element
key_idea_summary: An (r+1)-subset of {1, ..., n+1} with largest element k + 1 consists of that element together with an r-subset of {1, ..., k}; there are C(k, r) of them. Summing over k from r to n counts all C(n+1, r+1) subsets.
aliases: sum of C(k, r) over k

title: A Hypergraph with Fewer than 2^{k-1} Edges Is 2-Colourable
key_idea: colour each point by a fair coin; each set is monochromatic with probability 2^{1-k}, so the expected number of bad sets is less than 1
key_idea_summary: Under a uniformly random 2-colouring, a fixed k-set is monochromatic with probability 2 * 2^{-k} = 2^{1-k}. With m < 2^{k-1} sets the expected number of monochromatic sets is m 2^{1-k} < 1, so some colouring has none.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Summing Fixed Points over All Permutations (IMO 1987 Problem 1)
key_idea: the sum counts pairs (permutation, fixed point of it); count them by choosing the fixed point first
key_idea_summary: Each permutation with k fixed points contributes k pairs (permutation, fixed point), so the sum is the number of such pairs. Alternatively, choose the fixed point i (n ways) and then any permutation of the other n - 1 elements ((n-1)! ways): n (n-1)! = n! pairs.

title: At Most Six Unit Circles Can Touch a Given Unit Circle
key_idea: the centres of two touching circles subtend an angle of at least 60 degrees at the central circle's centre, and 360/60 = 6
key_idea_summary: The centres of the touching circles lie on a circle of radius 2 around the central centre O. Two touching circles that do not overlap have centres at distance at least 2, so the angle they subtend at O is at least 60 degrees (equilateral triangle). Non-overlapping angular sectors of at least 60 degrees each fit at most 360/60 = 6 times around O. The hexagonal arrangement achieves six.

title: Lattice Paths Are Binomial Coefficients
key_idea: a path is a word with m letters R and n letters U; choose the positions of the U's
key_idea_summary: Each path is a sequence of m + n steps of which exactly n are 'up'. Choosing which n of the m + n positions are up-steps determines the path, and there are C(m+n, n) such choices.
aliases: paths as words in R and U

title: No Lossless Compressor Shrinks Every File
key_idea: there are 2^n strings of length n but only 2^n - 1 strings of length less than n
key_idea_summary: Strings of length less than n number 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^{n-1} = 2^n - 1, fewer than the 2^n strings of length n. An injective compressor cannot map 2^n strings into 2^n - 1 targets, so some string of length n is not shortened. More generally, at most 2^{n-k+1} - 1 strings of length n can be compressed by k or more bits, a fraction about 2^{1-k}.

title: The Centre of a 3x3 Magic Square Is 5
key_idea: add the four lines through the centre: they cover every cell once and the centre four times
key_idea_summary: The magic sum is (1 + ... + 9)/3 = 15. The middle row, middle column and two diagonals together contain each cell once and the centre three extra times, so 4 * 15 = 45 + 3c, giving c = 5.

title: Mantel's Theorem, a Triangle-Free Graph Has at Most n^2/4 Edges

key_idea: for every edge uv, the neighbourhoods of u and v are disjoint, so d(u) + d(v) <= n; sum over edges
key_idea_summary: No triangle means an edge's two endpoints have no common neighbour, so d(u) + d(v) <= n for every edge uv. additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Rotating a Table of Misplaced Name Cards
key_idea: count the pairs (guest, rotation that seats them correctly): n pairs over n - 1 useful rotations
key_idea_summary: Each guest is correctly placed by exactly one of the n rotations, giving n correct placements in total. The zero rotation contributes none, so the other n - 1 rotations share n placements, and one of them has at least two.

title: The Monty Hall Problem

key_idea: your first pick is right with probability 1/3, and the host's action never changes that; switching wins exactly when the first pick was wrong
key_idea_summary: The first choice is correct with probability 1/3, wrong with probability 2/3. The host always opens a non-prize door, so the 'wrong' case leaves the prize behind the one remaining door. Switching therefore wins with probability 2/3.

title: Moser's Circle Problem, Regions Cut by Chords
key_idea: each region beyond the first is created by a chord or by a crossing, and crossings correspond to 4-subsets of the points
key_idea_summary: Add the chords one at a time: a chord crossing k earlier chords adds k + 1 regions. Summing, the total is 1 + (number of chords) + (number of crossings) = 1 + C(n,2) + C(n,4), because every crossing is determined by the four endpoints involved.
aliases: regions from chords between n points on a circle

title: Every Integer Has a Multiple Written with Only 0s and 1s

key_idea_summary: Among the n + 1 numbers 1, 11, ..., 111...1 (n + 1 ones) two have the same residue mod n. Their difference is 11...100...0, a multiple of n with digits 0 and 1.
aliases: multiple consisting of ones and zeros

title: Among n+1 Numbers from 1 to 2n, Two Are Coprime
key_idea: partition into the n pairs {1,2}, {3,4}, ..., {2n-1, 2n}; consecutive integers are coprime
key_idea_summary: With n boxes {2k-1, 2k} and n + 1 numbers, two chosen numbers fall into the same box, so they are consecutive and hence coprime.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Among n+1 Numbers from 1 to 2n, One Divides Another
key_idea: sort the numbers by their odd part
key_idea_summary: Write each chosen number as 2^k * m with m odd. There are only n odd numbers below 2n, so two chosen numbers share the same odd part m, and then the one with the smaller power of 2 divides the other.

title: Sum of Cubes Is the Square of the Sum (Nicomachus)
key_idea: expand the square as a sum over pairs (i, j) and group the pairs by max(i, j)
key_idea_summary: (1 + ... + n)^2 is the sum of i*j over all pairs (i, j) in {1..n}^2. The pairs with max(i, j) = k form an L-shaped gnomon whose total is k*(1 + ... + (k-1)) * 2 + k*k = k * k^2 = k^3.

title: A Graph without 4-Cycles Has at Most about n^{3/2}/2 Edges
key_idea: count 'cherries' (paths of length 2) in two ways: each pair of vertices has at most one common neighbour, so the number of cherries is at most C(n, 2); but each vertex v contributes C(d(v), 2) cherries

additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Among Six People, Three Mutual Acquaintances or Three Mutual Strangers
key_idea: one person has three relations of the same kind; then look at those three
key_idea_summary: Fix a person P. Of the other five, at least three are related to P in the same way, say acquainted. If any two of those three are acquainted, they form a triangle with P; if none are, the three are mutual strangers.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Pascal's Rule: Does the Subset Contain a Fixed Element?
key_idea: split the k-subsets of an n-set according to whether they contain a fixed element x
key_idea_summary: The k-subsets containing x correspond to (k-1)-subsets of the other n - 1 elements: C(n-1, k-1) of them. The k-subsets not containing x are k-subsets of the other n - 1 elements: C(n-1, k). Every k-subset is of exactly one kind.

title: A Planar Graph Has at Most 3V - 6 Edges

title: Every Planar Graph Has a Vertex of Degree at Most 5

title: Every Polyhedron Has Two Faces with the Same Number of Edges

key_idea_summary: Let F be a face with the maximum number of edges, m. Each of its m edges borders another face, giving m distinct neighbouring faces. Together with F there are m + 1 faces, each with between 3 and m edges: only m - 2 possible values, so two coincide.

title: Randomised Quicksort Makes about 2n ln n Comparisons
answer: 2 sum over i < j of 1/(j - i + 1) < 2n H_n
key_idea: the i-th and j-th smallest elements are compared iff one of them is the first pivot chosen among the elements between them, which happens with probability 2/(j - i + 1)
key_idea_summary: Two elements are compared at most once, and only when one of them is a pivot while both are still in the same sub-array. Consider the elements of ranks i, ..., j: the first of them to become a pivot separates the rest, and i and j are compared iff that first pivot is i or j itself, probability 2/(j - i + 1). Summing over pairs by linearity gives the bound.
additional_sources: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein - Introduction to Algorithms
aliases: elements i and j are compared with probability 2/(j - i + 1)

title: Erdos's Probabilistic Lower Bound for Ramsey Numbers
key_idea: colour every edge by a coin flip and show the expected number of monochromatic k-sets is less than 1
key_idea_summary: A fixed k-set is monochromatic with probability 2^{1 - C(k,2)}. There are C(n, k) k-sets, so the expected number of monochromatic ones is C(n,k) 2^{1 - C(k,2)}, which is less than 1 for n = 2^{k/2}. Some colouring therefore has none.

title: A Random Permutation Has One Fixed Point on Average
key_idea: write the count as a sum of n indicator variables, each with expectation 1/n
key_idea_summary: Let I_k be 1 if person k gets their own hat. Then the number of correct hats is I_1 + ... + I_n, and E[I_k] = 1/n. By linearity of expectation the total has expectation n * (1/n) = 1, even though the I_k are dependent.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: A Random Walk of n Steps Ends about sqrt(n) from the Start
key_idea: expand S_n^2 = sum of X_i^2 + 2 sum of X_i X_j; the squares are 1 and the cross terms have mean 0 by independence
key_idea_summary: Let S_n = X_1 + ... + X_n with independent X_i = +-1. Then S_n^2 = sum X_i^2 + 2 sum over i < j of X_i X_j. Each X_i^2 = 1 and E[X_i X_j] = E[X_i] E[X_j] = 0 for i != j. By linearity E[S_n^2] = n.
additional_sources: Feller - An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, vol. 1
aliases: variance of a sum of independent steps

title: The Rational Numbers Are Countable
key_idea: arrange the fractions p/q in a grid by (p, q) and walk through the grid along successive anti-diagonals
key_idea_summary: Place p/q at row p, column q. Each anti-diagonal p + q = s is finite, so listing the anti-diagonals in order s = 2, 3, 4, ... (skipping repeats) reaches every fraction after finitely many steps.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: The Expected Number of Records Is the Harmonic Number
key_idea: the k-th number is a record iff it is the largest of the first k, which has probability 1/k; add these up
key_idea_summary: Let I_k indicate that the k-th number is a record. Among the first k numbers each is equally likely to be the largest, so P(I_k = 1) = 1/k. By linearity, the expected number of records is the sum of 1/k.

title: Counting Rectangles on a Grid by Choosing Grid Lines
key_idea: a rectangle is exactly a choice of two of the nine horizontal grid lines and two of the nine vertical ones
key_idea_summary: The board has 9 horizontal and 9 vertical lines. A rectangle is determined by its top and bottom lines (a pair of horizontal lines) and its left and right lines (a pair of vertical lines), and every such choice gives a rectangle. So there are C(9, 2) * C(9, 2) = 1296 rectangles.
aliases: choose two horizontal and two vertical lines

title: A Regular Bipartite Graph Has Equally Many Vertices on Each Side
key_idea: count the dancing pairs from the boys' side and from the girls' side

title: Only Triangles, Squares and Hexagons Tile the Plane Regularly
key_idea: the interior angle 180(n - 2)/n must divide 360, which forces 2n/(n - 2) to be an integer
key_idea_summary: At a vertex of the tiling, k copies of the interior angle 180(n - 2)/n fill 360 degrees, so k = 2n/(n - 2) = 2 + 4/(n - 2) must be an integer. Then n - 2 divides 4, giving n = 3, 4 or 6 (with k = 6, 4, 3).

title: Two People at a Party Have the Same Number of Acquaintances
key_idea: the degrees 0 and n - 1 cannot both occur, leaving only n - 1 possible values for n people
key_idea_summary: Each person knows between 0 and n - 1 others, n possible values. But someone who knows nobody and someone who knows everybody cannot both be present, so at most n - 1 values occur among n people, and two coincide.

title: The Secretary Problem: Skip the First n/e Candidates
answer: reject about n/e candidates, then take the next best-so-far; success probability tends to 1/e = 0.368
key_idea: condition on the position k of the best candidate: the strategy wins iff the best of the first k - 1 lies among the first r, an event of probability r/(k - 1)
key_idea_summary: Condition on the position k of the best candidate. The strategy selects them iff the best of the first k - 1 candidates lies among the first r, which by symmetry has probability r/(k - 1). Summing over k gives P(win) = (r/n)(H_{n-1} - H_{r-1}), about (r/n) ln(n/r), which is maximised at r = n/e with value 1/e.
additional_sources: Ferguson - Who solved the secretary problem?
aliases: optimal stopping for the best candidate

title: Seven Real Numbers and the Tangent Subtraction Formula
key_idea: write each number as tan of an angle in (-90, 90) degrees; the expression is tan of the difference of angles
key_idea_summary: Put x_i = tan(t_i) with t_i in (-pi/2, pi/2). Then (x - y)/(1 + xy) = tan(t_x - t_y). Seven angles in an interval of length pi have two within pi/6 of each other, and tan of a difference in [0, pi/6] lies in [0, 1/sqrt(3)].

title: Seventeen Points, Three Colours, a Monochromatic Triangle
key_idea: apply pigeonhole twice: a vertex has 6 edges of one colour, and among those 6 endpoints the two-colour party-of-six argument applies
key_idea_summary: A fixed person has 16 correspondents, so at least 6 on the same topic A. If any two of those six use topic A we are done; otherwise they use only two topics, and among six people with two topics there is a monochromatic triangle by the friends-and-strangers theorem.

title: At Most 16 Non-Attacking Kings on a Chessboard
key_idea: cut the board into sixteen 2x2 blocks; any two squares of a block are adjacent, so each block holds at most one king
key_idea_summary: A king attacks all eight neighbouring squares, so two kings in the same 2x2 block attack each other. The board splits into 16 such blocks, giving at most 16 kings, and one king in the corner of each block achieves 16.

title: Sperner's Theorem on Antichains via Counting Maximal Chains (LYM)

key_idea: count the pairs (member of the antichain, maximal chain through it)
key_idea_summary: A maximal chain is an ordering of the n elements added one at a time; there are n! of them. A k-set lies on k!(n-k)! maximal chains, and a maximal chain passes through at most one member of an antichain. Hence sum over members of k!(n-k)! <= n!, i.e. sum of 1/C(n, |A|) <= 1, and since C(n, |A|) <= C(n, floor(n/2)) the antichain has at most C(n, floor(n/2)) members.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Sperner's Lemma via Counting Doors

Outer doors lie on the 1-2 side of the big triangle, where the colour changes an odd number of times. Counting door-ends two ways, the number of one-door rooms is odd, hence nonzero.

title: The Area of a Spherical Triangle (Girard's Theorem) via Lunes

The three lunes at A, B, C containing the triangle T, together with their antipodal copies, cover the sphere, with T and its antipode T' each covered three times and everything else once. Adding areas: 4(A + B + C) = 4 pi + 4 area(T).

title: How Many Squares Are on a Chessboard?

key_idea_summary: For each size k, the top-left cell of a k x k square must lie in the top-left (9 - k) x (9 - k) region, so there are (9 - k)^2 such squares. Summing over k = 1..8 gives 8^2 + 7^2 + ... + 1^2 = 204.

title: Stars and Bars

title: Among n Integers, Some Consecutive Block Sums to a Multiple of n

aliases: n integers subset sum divisible by n

title: A Set with n Elements Has 2^n Subsets
key_idea: a subset is a string of n yes/no decisions
key_idea_summary: Order the elements; a subset is determined by, and determines, the binary string recording which elements are in. There are 2^n binary strings of length n.

title: Every Set of Integers Has a Sum-Free Subset of at Least a Third of Its Size
key_idea: pick a prime p = 3k + 2 larger than all |a| and a random multiplier x; the elements a with xa mod p in the middle third (k+1..2k+1) form a sum-free set, and each element lands there with probability more than 1/3
key_idea_summary: Take a prime p = 3k + 2 larger than all |a| and the middle third M = {k+1, ..., 2k+1} of residues, which is sum-free mod p and makes up more than a third of the nonzero residues. For a random multiplier x, each xa mod p lands in M with probability above 1/3, so on average more than n/3 elements land there, and those elements form a sum-free set because dilation preserves sums.

title: The Sum of Squares of Binomial Coefficients
key_idea: choose n objects from n red and n blue ones, classified by how many are red; or count lattice paths by where they cross the middle anti-diagonal
key_idea_summary: C(2n, n) counts n-subsets of a set of n red and n blue objects. A subset with k red objects has n - k blue ones, and there are C(n, k) C(n, n-k) = C(n,k)^2 such subsets. Summing over k gives the identity.

title: The Sum of the Reciprocals of the Primes Diverges (Erdos's Proof)
key_idea: if the tail sum over 'large' primes were less than 1/2, then for a huge N fewer than N/2 integers up to N would have a large prime factor, but the integers with only small prime factors number at most 2^k sqrt N, which is also less than N/2 for large N
key_idea_summary: If the sum converged, some k would make the sum of 1/p over primes beyond p_k less than 1/2; call those primes large. Up to N, fewer than N/2 integers have a large prime factor, while integers with only small prime factors are a square-free part (2^k choices) times a square (sqrt N choices): at most 2^k sqrt N. For N = 2^{2k+2} this is N/2, so the two classes cannot cover all N integers.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK
aliases: Erdos's proof of the divergence of prime reciprocals

title: Counting Onto Functions by Inclusion-Exclusion
answer: sum over j of (-1)^j C(k, j) (k - j)^n
key_idea: count all functions and subtract those missing at least one target value, using inclusion-exclusion over the set of missed values
key_idea_summary: Let A_i be the set of functions whose image misses value i. Functions missing a prescribed set of j values number (k - j)^n. By inclusion-exclusion the number of functions missing no value is sum over j of (-1)^j C(k, j)(k - j)^n.

title: Ten Two-Digit Numbers Contain Two Disjoint Subsets with Equal Sums
key_idea: there are more subsets than possible sums
key_idea_summary: The set has 2^10 - 1 = 1023 non-empty subsets, but any subset sum is at most 91 + 92 + ... + 99 + 90 < 1000. Two subsets share a sum; removing their common elements leaves two disjoint subsets with equal sums.

title: Number of Matches in a Knockout Tournament
key_idea: matches correspond one-to-one to losers
key_idea_summary: Every match produces exactly one loser and every player except the champion loses exactly once. So matches are in bijection with the n - 1 non-champions.

title: A 2-Coloured 3x7 Grid Contains a Monochromatic Rectangle
key_idea: a column of three cells has two of the same colour; there are only 6 such (pair of rows, colour) patterns for 7 columns
key_idea_summary: Each column has a majority colour occupying at least two of its three cells; record the colour and a pair of rows carrying it: at most 2 * 3 = 6 possibilities. Two of the seven columns share the record, and their four cells form a monochromatic rectangle.
aliases: monochromatic rectangle in a coloured grid

title: The Three Utilities Problem: K_{3,3} Is Not Planar
key_idea: Euler's formula plus the fact that every face of a bipartite plane graph has at least 4 edges
key_idea_summary: A planar drawing of K_{3,3} would have V = 6, E = 9, hence F = 2 - 6 + 9 = 5 faces by Euler. K_{3,3} is bipartite, so it has no triangles and every face is bounded by at least 4 edges; counting edge-face incidences, 4F <= 2E, i.e. 20 <= 18. Contradiction.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Counting Winning Lines in 3D Tic-Tac-Toe (Moser's Shell)

key_idea: extend each line one step beyond the cube and count the shell cells it hits
key_idea_summary: Surround the 8x8x8 cube by a shell of unit cells, making a 10x10x10 cube. Extending a winning line by one cell at each end lands in exactly two shell cells, and every shell cell is hit by exactly one line. Winning lines are therefore in bijection with pairs of shell cells, so there are (10^3 - 8^3)/2 of them.
aliases: number of lines in an n x n x n tic-tac-toe cube

title: Toads and Frogs Takes Exactly MN + M + N Moves
answer: MN jumps and M + N slides, MN + M + N moves in all
key_idea: count total displacement and count crossings
key_idea_summary: Each frog must end M + 1 squares to the right and each toad N + 1 squares to the left, a total displacement of N(M+1) + M(N+1) = 2MN + M + N. Every frog-toad pair crosses exactly once, and only by a jump (displacement 2), giving MN jumps; the remaining displacement M + N must come from slides (displacement 1).

title: The Sum of phi(d) over Divisors d of n Equals n
key_idea: the fractions 1/n, 2/n, ..., n/n, written in lowest terms, have denominators dividing n, and exactly phi(d) of them have denominator d
key_idea_summary: Reduce each of the n fractions k/n (1 <= k <= n) to lowest terms a/d. The denominator d divides n, and the fractions with denominator d are exactly the a/d with 1 <= a <= d and gcd(a, d) = 1, phi(d) of them. Summing over d counts all n fractions.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK
aliases: sum of Euler's phi over divisors

title: Tournaments in Which Every k Players Are Beaten by Someone (Erdos)

key_idea: orient each edge by a coin flip; a fixed k-set is left undominated with probability (1 - 2^{-k})^{n-k}, which decays exponentially in n
key_idea_summary: In a random tournament on n players, a fixed player beats all of a given k-set with probability 2^{-k}, so none of the other n - k players does with probability (1 - 2^{-k})^{n-k}. There are C(n, k) k-sets, and C(n,k)(1 - 2^{-k})^{n-k} < 1 for n large, so some tournament has no undominated k-set.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Trailing Zeros of n! by Counting Multiples of 5
key_idea: count factors of 5, since factors of 2 are plentiful; count multiples of 5, of 25, of 125, ... and add

title: Ten Points in an Equilateral Triangle of Side 1

title: Vandermonde's Identity by Choosing a Committee

title: The Babylonian Square Root Iteration Converges
key_idea: after one step the iterates are above sqrt(a) by AM-GM, and from then on they decrease
key_idea_summary: x_{n+1} is the arithmetic mean of x_n and a/x_n, whose geometric mean is sqrt(a); so x_{n+1} >= sqrt(a) for n >= 0. Once x_n >= sqrt(a), a/x_n <= x_n, so x_{n+1} <= x_n. A decreasing sequence bounded below converges, and the limit L satisfies L = (L + a/L)/2, i.e. L = sqrt(a).

title: Benford's Law for Powers of Two via Rotation of the Circle
answer: Frequency of leading digit d is log10(1 + 1/d): 30.1% for 1, 17.6% for 2, ..., 4.6% for 9.
key_idea: take log10; the leading digit is read off from the position on a circle that rotates by an irrational angle
key_idea_summary: 2^n has leading digit d exactly when the fractional part of n*log10(2) lies in [log10(d), log10(d+1)). The fractional parts of n*alpha for irrational alpha are equidistributed on the circle [0,1), so the frequency equals the length of that arc, log10(1 + 1/d).
aliases: leading digit of powers of two

title: Iterating the Cosine Converges from Any Start
answer: converges to the unique solution of cos x = x, approximately 0.7391
key_idea: after one step the values lie in [-1, 1], where |cos'(x)| = |sin x| <= sin 1 < 1, so cosine is a contraction there
key_idea_summary: After the first step all iterates lie in [-1, 1], and on that interval the derivative of cosine is bounded by sin 1 = 0.84 < 1. By the mean value theorem consecutive differences shrink by at least this factor, so the sequence is Cauchy and converges to a fixed point, which is unique for the same reason.

title: The Four-Number Game (Ducci Sequence) Always Reaches Zero
key_idea: modulo 2 the map is linear and nilpotent: after four steps everything is even, then rescale
key_idea_summary: Modulo 2, |x - y| = x + y, so the step is the linear map I + S with S the cyclic shift, and (I + S)^4 = I + S^4 = 0 mod 2: after 4 steps all entries are even. Halving commutes with the step and the maximum never increases, so after 4k steps all entries are multiples of 2^k bounded by the original maximum, hence eventually 0.

title: Fibonacci Numbers Modulo m Are Purely Periodic
key_idea: the step (a, b) -> (b, a + b) is an invertible map on a finite set
key_idea_summary: The pair of consecutive residues (F_n, F_{n+1}) mod m determines all later pairs, and there are only m^2 possible pairs, so the sequence of pairs eventually repeats. The step map is invertible (its inverse is (a, b) -> (b - a, a)), so the repetition must include the very first pair (0, 1), which then recurs forever.

title: Cycle Detection with a Tortoise and a Hare

key_idea: once both are on the cycle, the hare gains one position per step on the tortoise, so it laps it within one cycle length
key_idea_summary: Let the sequence become periodic with period L after mu steps. For i >= mu both x_i and x_{2i} are on the cycle, and x_{2i} = x_i exactly when L divides 2i - i = i. title: Kaprekar's Routine Always Reaches 6174

key_idea: the result of one step depends only on the multiset of digits, and only on the three digit differences; this collapses 10,000 starting values to a few dozen states of a finite dynamical system whose only cycle is the fixed point 6174

title: Eight Perfect Shuffles Restore a Deck of 52 Cards

title: The Period of 1/p Is the Order of 10 Modulo p

title: The Values sin 1, sin 2, sin 3, ... Are Dense in [-1, 1]

title: 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n Is Never an Integer
