title: One Straight Cut Bisects Two Pancakes Simultaneously
key_idea: for each direction there is a unique line in that direction bisecting the first region; as the direction rotates by 180 degrees, the signed excess of the second region on the left of that line changes sign
key_idea_summary: For each direction t let L(t) be the line in that direction bisecting region A, which moves continuously with t. Let g(t) be the area of B to the left of L(t) minus the area to the right. Rotating by 180 degrees gives the same line with the sides swapped, so g(t + 180) = -g(t), and the intermediate value theorem gives a direction with g = 0, where L(t) bisects both regions.
aliases: ham sandwich theorem in the plane
bisecting two regions with one line

title: Pompeiu's Theorem by Rotation
key_idea: rotate by 60 degrees about a vertex; the three distances become the sides of one triangle
key_idea_summary: Rotate the plane by 60 degrees about A, taking B to C and P to P'. Then AP = AP' = PP' (equilateral triangle APP'), and CP' = BP. So triangle PP'C has sides PP' = PA, P'C = PB and PC.
aliases: distances to vertices of an equilateral triangle form a triangle

title: Ptolemy's Theorem by Inversion
key_idea: invert in a circle centred at A: the circumcircle becomes a line through the images of B, C, D, and distances transform by a known formula, so 'collinear' (B'C' + C'D' = B'D') becomes Ptolemy's equation
key_idea_summary: Invert about A: the circumcircle, passing through A, becomes a line on which B', C', D' lie in order, so B'D' = B'C' + C'D'. Distances transform as P'Q' = r^2 PQ/(AP * AQ), and substituting and clearing denominators turns this collinearity into AC * BD = AB * CD + AD * BC.
aliases: AC * BD = AB * CD + AD * BC

title: A Triangular Prism Splits into Three Pyramids of Equal Volume
key_idea: cut the prism into three tetrahedra that pairwise share a base and a height
key_idea_summary: Cut the prism ABC-A'B'C' into the tetrahedra A'ABC, A'B'C'C and A'BCB'. The first two have congruent bases (the two triangular faces) and the prism's height; the last two share the apex A' and have as bases the two halves of the parallelogram face BCC'B'. So all three have equal volume, one third of the prism.
aliases: volume of a pyramid is one third

title: The Pythagorean Theorem by Similarity and Scaling
key_idea: the altitude to the hypotenuse cuts the triangle into two triangles similar to it, and areas of similar figures scale with the square of any corresponding length
key_idea_summary: The altitude from the right angle splits the triangle into two smaller right triangles, each similar to the whole, with hypotenuses a and b. A right triangle of a given shape has area k times the square of its hypotenuse, for a constant k depending only on the shape. Adding the two small areas gives k a^2 + k b^2 = k c^2.
aliases: Einstein's proof of the Pythagorean theorem
altitude splits the triangle into similar copies

title: A Quadrilateral Has an Incircle Iff Opposite Sides Have Equal Sums (Pitot)
key_idea: the two tangent segments from each vertex to the circle are equal, so each side splits into two tangent lengths and the four lengths pair off oppositely
key_idea_summary: From a point outside a circle the two tangent segments are equal. Label the tangent lengths from the four vertices p, q, r, s. Then the sides are p + q, q + r, r + s, s + p, and (p + q) + (r + s) = (q + r) + (s + p): opposite sides have equal sums.

title: The Shortest Curve Bisecting an Equilateral Triangle Is a Circular Arc
answer: an arc of a circle centred at a vertex, of radius such that the sector has half the triangle's area
key_idea: reflect the triangle repeatedly around a vertex to form a regular hexagon; a curve cutting off a corner region of the triangle becomes, with its five reflections, a closed curve in the hexagon, and the isoperimetric inequality makes the circle optimal
key_idea_summary: A bisecting curve cutting off a region at vertex A, together with its five images under reflection of the triangle around A, forms a closed curve in a regular hexagon enclosing half the hexagon. The isoperimetric inequality says the shortest such closed curve is a circle centred at A, so the shortest bisector is a circular arc, which beats both the altitude and the parallel chord.

title: The Shortest Fence Halving a Quarter-Circle Pasture
answer: an arc of a circle centred at the corner (the centre of the quarter-disc), of radius R/sqrt(2)
key_idea: reflect the quarter-disc in its two straight edges to get a full disc; the fence and its reflections form a closed curve of four times the length enclosing half the disc's area, and the isoperimetric inequality says the shortest such curve is a circle
key_idea_summary: Reflecting in both radii turns the quarter-disc into a full disc and the fence into a closed curve of four times the fence's length, enclosing four times the fenced area, namely half of the disc. Among closed curves enclosing a given area the circle is shortest (isoperimetric inequality), and the circle enclosing half the disc's area is concentric with radius R/sqrt(2). Its quarter, an arc centred at the corner, is therefore the shortest fence.
aliases: shortest fence in a quarter-circle pasture
bisecting a quadrant with a curve of least length

title: The Volume of a Sphere by Cavalieri's Principle
key_idea: at every height, the cross-section of a hemisphere has the same area as the cross-section of a cylinder with a cone removed
key_idea_summary: At height h a hemisphere of radius r is cut in a disc of area pi(r^2 - h^2), while a cylinder of radius r and height r with an inverted cone removed is cut in an annulus of the same area pi r^2 - pi h^2. Equal slices at every height give equal volumes: pi r^3 - pi r^3/3 = 2 pi r^3/3 for the hemisphere.
aliases: volume of a ball is 4/3 pi r^3

title: The Spider and the Fly
key_idea: unfold the room into a flat net and draw a straight line
key_idea_summary: A path on the surface of a box becomes a straight segment when the box is unfolded along the faces the path crosses. Trying the different nets, the shortest straight-line distance is sqrt(32^2 + 24^2) = 40, achieved by a path that visits five of the six faces.
aliases: shortest path on the surface of a box

title: The Centre of a Circle Cannot Be Found with a Straightedge Alone
key_idea: a projective transformation maps the circle to a circle (a suitable central projection between planes) but moves its centre; straightedge constructions are preserved by projective maps
key_idea_summary: Any straightedge construction uses only points, lines through two points and intersections of lines, all of which are preserved by projective transformations. There is a projective map taking the given circle to itself (as a set) but not fixing its centre. Applying it to a supposed construction would produce the same construction with a different 'centre': contradiction.

title: The Shortest Path around a Cylinder
key_idea: unroll the cylinder into a rectangle; the string becomes a straight line
key_idea_summary: Cut the cylinder along a vertical line and unroll it into a 4 x 12 rectangle; going once around the cylinder becomes crossing the rectangle horizontally. Four turns over the full height unroll to a straight line from corner to corner of a 16 x 12 rectangle (four rectangles side by side), of length sqrt(16^2 + 12^2) = 20.

title: The Angle Sum of an n-gon by Triangulation from a Vertex
key_idea: draw all diagonals from one vertex: the polygon splits into n - 2 triangles whose angles together make up the polygon's angles
key_idea_summary: From a fixed vertex, the n - 3 diagonals cut the convex polygon into n - 2 triangles. Every angle of these triangles is part of an angle of the polygon and the triangle angles exactly fill the polygon's angles, so the total is (n - 2) * 180.

title: The Sum of the First n Odd Numbers Is n^2
key_idea: an n x n square of dots is a nest of L-shaped layers with 1, 3, 5, ... dots
key_idea_summary: Build the n x n square by adding an L-shaped border to the (n-1) x (n-1) square; the border has (n-1) + (n-1) + 1 = 2n - 1 dots. So the square is the sum of the first n odd numbers.
aliases: proof without words for odd numbers

title: The Volume of the Regular Tetrahedron in a Cube
key_idea: the cube is the tetrahedron plus four congruent corner pyramids, each of volume 1/6
key_idea_summary: Removing the tetrahedron from the cube leaves four congruent right-corner pyramids, each with three mutually perpendicular unit edges, hence of volume (1/3) * (1/2) * 1 = 1/6. So the tetrahedron has volume 1 - 4/6 = 1/3.
aliases: volume one third of the cube

title: The Angle in a Semicircle Is Right (Thales)
key_idea: join C to the centre: the radius splits the triangle into two isosceles triangles whose base angles add up to the angle at C
key_idea_summary: Let O be the centre. OA = OB = OC, so triangles OAC and OBC are isosceles with base angles a and b. The angles of triangle ABC are a, b and a + b, and their sum is 180, so a + b = 90.

title: Two Consecutive Triangular Numbers Sum to a Square
key_idea: cut an n x n square of dots along its diagonal: the diagonal and one side form a staircase of T_n dots, the other side a staircase of T_{n-1} dots
key_idea_summary: Draw an n x n array of dots and separate the dots on or below the main diagonal from those strictly above it. The first set is a staircase with rows of lengths 1, 2, ..., n, i.e. T_n dots; the second is a staircase with rows of lengths 1, ..., n - 1, i.e. T_{n-1} dots. Together they make n^2.

title: Viviani's Theorem
key_idea: split the triangle into three triangles with the point as apex and compare areas
key_idea_summary: Joining the interior point P to the vertices cuts the triangle into three triangles whose bases are the sides (all of length s) and whose heights are the three distances. Their areas add to the whole area (1/2) s h, so (1/2) s (d_1 + d_2 + d_3) = (1/2) s h.
aliases: sum of distances to the sides of an equilateral triangle
constant distance sum in an equilateral triangle

title: A Wobbly Four-Legged Table Can Be Stabilised by Rotating It
answer: proved (rotation by at most 90 degrees suffices)
key_idea: track the height of the hovering leg as the table rotates; after a quarter turn the roles of the legs swap and the height changes sign
key_idea_summary: Rest three legs on the ground and let h(t) be the signed height of the fourth leg above the ground at rotation angle t (negative if it would have to go below ground). Rotating by 90 degrees brings the table into the same set of positions with a different leg free, and one checks that h(90) has the opposite sign to h(0). By continuity h vanishes at some angle in between, where all four legs touch.
additional_sources: Gardner - The Colossal Book of Short Puzzles and Problems

title: Young's Inequality from Two Areas
key_idea: the rectangle [0, a] x [0, b] is covered by the region under y = x^{p-1} from 0 to a and the region to the left of x = y^{q-1} from 0 to b
key_idea_summary: The curve y = x^{p-1} is the same as x = y^{q-1}, since (p - 1)(q - 1) = 1. The area under it from 0 to a is a^p/p, and the area between it and the y-axis from 0 to b is b^q/q. Together the two regions cover the rectangle of area ab, with equality exactly when the curve passes through the corner (a, b), i.e. b = a^{p-1}.
aliases: areas under a curve and its inverse

title: Iterating Arithmetic and Harmonic Means Converges to the Geometric Mean
answer: both converge to sqrt(ab), the geometric mean
key_idea: the product ab is invariant, while the gap closes
key_idea_summary: The arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean is exactly ab, so the product never changes. The larger number decreases and the smaller increases at every step, and their difference at least halves, so they converge to a common value L with L^2 = ab.
aliases: product is invariant under mean iteration

title: Binary Search Is Correct: an Invariant and a Halving Monovariant
key_idea: the invariant 'if the target is in the array, it is in lo..hi' is preserved, and the interval length at least halves each step
key_idea_summary: Comparing the target with the middle element m tells, by sortedness, that the target cannot lie left of m (if target > a[m]) or right of m (if target < a[m]); discarding that part preserves the invariant. The interval length shrinks from L to at most floor(L/2), so after about log_2 n steps the interval is empty (target absent) or the middle element equals the target.
additional_sources: Knuth - The Art of Computer Programming, vol. 3

title: Breaking a Chocolate Bar
answer: exactly mn - 1 breaks, regardless of the order
key_idea: count pieces, not breaks
key_idea_summary: Every break increases the number of pieces by exactly one. Starting from one piece and ending with mn pieces therefore takes exactly mn - 1 breaks, whatever strategy is used.
aliases: minimum number of breaks of a chocolate bar

title: Brussels Sprouts Always Lasts Exactly 5n - 2 Moves
answer: always 5n - 2 moves; the first player wins iff n is odd
key_idea: the number of free arms never changes (each move uses two and creates two), and Euler's formula for the final planar map fixes the number of moves
key_idea_summary: Every move consumes two free arms and creates two, so there are always 4n free arms, and the game ends when each face of the drawing contains exactly one of them: 4n faces. After m moves there are n + m vertices and 2m edges, so Euler's formula (n + m) - 2m + 4n = 2 gives m = 5n - 2.
additional_sources: Berlekamp, Conway, Guy - Winning Ways for Your Mathematical Plays

title: Chameleons of Three Colours
key_idea: differences of the colour counts are invariant modulo 3
key_idea_summary: A meeting changes the counts by (-1, -1, +2) in some order, so every pairwise difference changes by 0 or +-3: the differences are invariant mod 3. Initially all differences are nonzero mod 3, while a single-colour state has two differences equal to 0 mod 3.

title: Check Digits Detect Every Single-Digit Error
key_idea: a single change alters the weighted sum by w * (d' - d) with weight w = 1 or 3, which is nonzero mod 10 since w is coprime to 10 and |d' - d| < 10; transpositions change it by 2(d - d'), invisible when d - d' = 5
key_idea_summary: A valid code has weighted sum 0 mod 10. Changing one digit changes the sum by w(d' - d) with w in {1, 3} coprime to 10 and 0 < |d' - d| < 10, so the sum leaves 0 mod 10: detected. Swapping adjacent digits changes it by 2(d - d'), invisible exactly when the digits differ by 5. With the prime modulus 11 and weights 1..10 (ISBN-10) both kinds of error are always detected.

title: A Number Minus Its Digit Reversal Is Divisible by 9
key_idea: a number is congruent to its digit sum modulo 9, and permuting digits does not change the digit sum
key_idea_summary: Since 10 = 1 mod 9, every number is congruent mod 9 to the sum of its digits. Reversing the digits leaves the digit sum unchanged, so the two numbers are congruent mod 9 and their difference is divisible by 9.

title: Iterated Digit Sums of 4444^4444 (IMO 1975 Problem 4)
key_idea: taking the digit sum preserves the residue mod 9, and crude size bounds pin the answer down
key_idea_summary: Since 10 = 1 mod 9, a number and its digit sum are congruent mod 9. So the digit sum of B is congruent to 4444^4444 = 7^4444 = 7 mod 9. Size bounds show B < 100 and its digit sum is at most 18, and the only such number that is 7 mod 9 is 7.
aliases: sum of digits of the sum of digits

title: Divisibility by 11 and the Alternating Digit Sum
key_idea_summary: A number is sum of d_k 10^k. Since 10 = -1 mod 11, 10^k = (-1)^k mod 11, so the number is congruent to d_0 - d_1 + d_2 - ... mod 11. Divisibility of the number is therefore equivalent to divisibility of the alternating digit sum.

title: Killing the Dragon (Heads Mod 3)
key_idea: the number of heads modulo 3 never changes
key_idea_summary: The four blows change the head count by +9, -15, -6 and +12, all multiples of 3. Since 100 is not a multiple of 3, the count can never reach 0.

title: The Exterior Angles of a Convex Polygon Sum to 360 Degrees
key_idea: walk around the polygon: the total turning is one full revolution
key_idea_summary: Walk along the boundary. At each vertex you turn through the exterior angle. After going all the way around you face your original direction again, having turned exactly 360 degrees in total. Each interior angle is 180 minus the exterior one, so the interior angles sum to 180n - 360.

title: Fifteen Puzzle (Sam Loyd's 14-15 Puzzle)
key_idea: parity of the permutation, corrected by the blank's position
key_idea_summary: Treat the blank as a 16th tile. Each move is a transposition of the blank with a neighbour, so it flips the sign of the permutation and changes the blank's taxicab distance from its home corner by one. The product sign x (-1)^distance is therefore invariant; swapping 14 and 15 alone changes it.

title: Gambler's Ruin in a Fair Game by Conservation of Expected Fortune
key_idea: in a fair game the expected fortune is conserved, so the final expected fortune equals the initial fortune k
key_idea_summary: Each bet has expected gain 0, so the expected fortune stays k throughout, including at the (random) end of play. At the end the fortune is N with probability p and 0 with probability 1 - p, so pN = k and p = k/N.
additional_sources: Feller - An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, vol. 1

title: The Area under 1/x Is Additive under Scaling
key_idea: stretching the region horizontally by k and squashing it vertically by 1/k is an area-preserving map that carries the region over [a, b] to the region over [ka, kb]
key_idea_summary: The map (x, y) -> (kx, y/k) multiplies areas by k * (1/k) = 1 and sends the point (x, 1/x) on the hyperbola to (kx, 1/(kx)), again on the hyperbola. So it maps the region under the curve between a and b onto the region between ka and kb, and the areas agree. Then L(xy) = A(1, xy) = A(1, x) + A(x, xy) = A(1, x) + A(1, y).
aliases: logarithm from areas under the hyperbola

title: Nim and the Binary Digital Sum
answer: The player to move loses exactly when the bitwise XOR (nim-sum) of the heap sizes is 0; otherwise a winning move is one that makes the nim-sum 0.
key_idea: encode heaps in binary and track the XOR
key_idea_summary: Write heap sizes in binary and XOR them column-wise. From nim-sum 0 every move produces a nonzero nim-sum, and from nonzero nim-sum some move restores 0. Since the terminal position has nim-sum 0, the player facing nim-sum 0 loses.
additional_sources: Berlekamp, Conway, Guy - Winning Ways for Your Mathematical Plays

title: Peg Solitaire and the Klein Four-Group
answer: Only at the centre or at one of the four holes three steps from the centre along a row or column (five positions in all).
key_idea: label holes with elements of the Klein four-group
key_idea_summary: Label hole (x,y) with A, B or C according to (x+y) mod 3, where A, B, C are the non-identity elements of the Klein four-group (AB = C, each element its own inverse). Three consecutive holes carry all three labels, so a jump replaces two labels by their product and the product over occupied holes is invariant. A second labelling by (x-y) mod 3 pins the last peg down to five holes.
aliases: English peg solitaire final peg positions

title: The Five Tips of a Pentagram Have Angles Summing to 180 Degrees
key_idea: walking around the star, the direction of travel turns through two full revolutions, so the exterior angles sum to 720 and the interior tip angles to 5 * 180 - 720
key_idea_summary: Traverse the five edges of the star in order. At each tip the direction turns by 180 - (tip angle). Since the star winds twice around its centre, the total turning is 2 * 360 = 720 degrees. So sum of (180 - tip angle) = 720, i.e. the tip angles sum to 900 - 720 = 180.

title: In Polya's Urn the Colour Proportions Never Drift
key_idea: the expected fraction of red balls is conserved by each step (it is a martingale), and the probability of a red draw equals that expected fraction
key_idea_summary: If the red fraction is p before a draw, the expected red fraction after the draw is again p: the two possible outcomes average out exactly. So the expected fraction is conserved (a martingale), and the probability that draw n is red equals the expected fraction before it, r/(r + b).
additional_sources: Feller - An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, vol. 1
aliases: probability the n-th ball is red

title: In Every Pythagorean Triple, 3, 4 and 5 Divide a Side
key_idea: squares take few values modulo 3, 4 (or 8) and 5, and the equation is impossible unless one of the variables carries the zero residue
key_idea_summary: Squares are 0 or 1 mod 3, so two legs not divisible by 3 give a^2 + b^2 = 2 mod 3, not a square. Squares are 0, 1, 4 mod 5, and if none of a, b, c is a multiple of 5 no combination fits. Odd squares are 1 mod 8: both legs odd is impossible, and with one even leg a^2 = c^2 - b^2 = 0 mod 8 gives 4 | a.

title: Sign Flips of Rows and Columns Preserve the Product of Any Rectangle's Corners
answer: invariant proved; the single -1 grid cannot be cleared, since a rectangle containing that corner has corner product -1 while the all-ones grid gives +1
key_idea: each row or column flip changes exactly two of the four corners of any rectangle
key_idea_summary: A row flip changes the two corners lying in that row (or none), a column flip the two corners in that column. Two sign changes leave the product unchanged. The all-+1 grid has all corner products +1, so any grid with some rectangle of corner product -1 is unreachable.
aliases: row and column sign flips invariant

title: Reservoir Sampling: Keep the k-th Item with Probability 1/k
key_idea: the invariant 'the stored item is uniform among the items seen so far' is preserved by each replacement step
key_idea_summary: Suppose after k - 1 arrivals the stored item is uniform among them, each with probability 1/(k - 1). The k-th item replaces it with probability 1/k, and otherwise (probability (k - 1)/k) the old item stays, so each earlier item now has probability (1/(k - 1)) * ((k - 1)/k) = 1/k, the same as the new item. The invariant holds for all k by induction.
additional_sources: Knuth - The Art of Computer Programming, vol. 2

title: Replacing (a, b) by (0.6a - 0.8b, 0.8a + 0.6b)
key_idea: the move is a rotation, so the sum of squares is invariant
key_idea_summary: (0.6a - 0.8b)^2 + (0.8a + 0.6b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 because 0.36 + 0.64 = 1 and the cross terms cancel; the move rotates the point (a, b) about the origin. The sum of the three squares is therefore invariant: 169 at the start, 196 at the target.
aliases: rotation moves on a triple of numbers

title: A Single Flipped Edge on a Rubik's Cube Is Unsolvable
key_idea: the sum of the edge orientations modulo 2 is invariant under every face turn
key_idea_summary: Mark each edge piece with an orientation bit relative to a fixed convention. A quarter turn of a face moves four edges and flips the orientation bits of an even number of them (0 or 4 depending on the convention), so the total orientation mod 2 is invariant. A single flipped edge has total 1, while the solved cube has total 0.

title: Splitting Piles and Summing Products
answer: proved; the total is always n(n-1)/2
key_idea: each product counts the threads cut between the two parts
key_idea_summary: Join every pair of chips by a thread: n(n-1)/2 threads. Splitting a pile into parts of sizes x and y cuts exactly xy threads. Every thread is cut exactly once by the end, so the products add up to the number of threads.

title: Sums of Two Squares Are Never 3 mod 4
key_idea: reduce modulo a small modulus where squares take few values
key_idea_summary: Squares are 0 or 1 mod 4, so a sum of two squares is 0, 1 or 2 mod 4, never 3. Differences of squares are 0, 1 or 3 mod 4, never 2. Modulo 10 the squares end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9 only.

title: Splitting Piles into Piles of Three
key_idea: stones plus piles is invariant
key_idea_summary: A move removes one stone and adds one pile, so (number of stones) + (number of piles) is constant, equal to 1002. A position with k piles of 3 has 3k + k = 4k, and 1002 is not divisible by 4.
additional_sources: Fomin, Genkin, Itenberg - Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience)

title: Numbers 4 or 5 mod 9 Are Not Sums of Three Cubes
key_idea: cubes are 0, 1 or -1 modulo 9
key_idea_summary: Every integer is 0, +-1, +-2, +-3 or +-4 mod 9, and cubing these gives only 0, 1 and -1 mod 9. A sum of three such values lies between -3 and 3 mod 9, so it is never 4 or 5.

title: The Sum of Two Odd Squares Is Never a Square
key_idea: odd squares are 1 mod 4, so the sum is 2 mod 4, but squares are 0 or 1 mod 4
key_idea_summary: (2m + 1)^2 = 4m(m + 1) + 1 = 1 mod 4 (in fact mod 8). Two odd squares sum to 2 mod 4, and no square is 2 mod 4.
aliases: a^2 + b^2 with a, b odd

title: Sums and Products (Replace a, b by ab + a + b)
answer: (n+1)! - 1, independent of the order of moves
key_idea: the product of (x + 1) over all numbers on the board is invariant
key_idea_summary: Since ab + a + b + 1 = (a+1)(b+1), replacing a, b by ab + a + b leaves the product of (x+1) over the board unchanged. At the end that product is (final + 1), and at the start it is 2 * 3 * ... * (n+1).

title: Three Pegs Sliding Parallel to the Opposite Side
key_idea: the area of the triangle is invariant
key_idea_summary: Moving a vertex parallel to the opposite side keeps the base and the height, hence the area, fixed. The initial area is 9/2, the target area is 4.

title: Flipping 2x2 Blocks Preserves Every Row Product
key_idea: a 2x2 flip changes exactly two entries in each of two rows, so the product of every row is invariant
key_idea_summary: A 2x2 block meets two rows in two cells each. Flipping it multiplies each of those row products by (-1)^2 = 1. So all row products are invariant; the row containing the -1 has product -1 forever, while the all-+1 grid has all row products +1.
additional_sources: Fomin, Genkin, Itenberg - Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience)
aliases: single minus one cannot be removed by block flips

title: Wine in the Water Glass Equals Water in the Wine Glass
key_idea: each glass ends with its original volume, so whatever wine left the wine glass was replaced by an equal volume of water
key_idea_summary: After the two transfers each glass again holds its original volume. The wine missing from the wine glass has been replaced, volume for volume, by water; so the water in the wine glass equals the wine in the water glass. Stirring, spoon size and even the number of transfers are irrelevant.
additional_sources: Gardner - The Colossal Book of Short Puzzles and Problems

title: Candy Sharing in a Circle Equalises
key_idea: the maximum never increases, the minimum never decreases, and the number of minimum-holders shrinks
key_idea_summary: After a whistle each student holds the average of two even numbers, which lies between the old minimum m and maximum M; the extra candy cannot push anyone above M (M is even). So M never increases, m never decreases, and unless everyone holds m, the set of students holding m strictly shrinks; when it empties, m rises by at least 2.
aliases: pass half your candy to the right

title: Chebyshev's Sum Inequality from the Rearrangement Inequality
key_idea: expand the right side as n sums of products a_i b_{sigma(i)} over the n cyclic shifts, each of which is at most the sorted sum by rearrangement
key_idea_summary: The product of the two sums is the sum over all pairs of a_i b_j, which can be grouped into the n cyclic pairings j = i + k mod n. Each cyclic pairing is a rearrangement of the b's, so its sum is at most the similarly ordered sum. Adding the n bounds gives the inequality.
aliases: average of products versus product of averages

title: Conway's Soldiers (Sending Scouts into the Desert)
answer: Rows 1 to 4 above the line can be reached; row 5 cannot, however many checkers are used.
key_idea: a golden-ratio weighting whose total never increases
key_idea_summary: Give the cell at distance d (taxicab) from the target the weight phi^{-d}, where phi is the golden ratio; since phi^{-2} + phi^{-1} = 1, a jump toward the target never increases the total weight and other jumps decrease it. The whole half-plane below the line has total weight exactly 1 when the target is in row 5, so a checker (weight 1) can never arrive there.
additional_sources: Berlekamp, Conway, Guy - Winning Ways for Your Mathematical Plays

title: The Cut Property: the Cheapest Edge across Any Cut Belongs to a Minimum Spanning Tree
key_idea: add the light edge to any spanning tree not containing it; this closes a cycle that crosses the cut somewhere else, and swapping out that other crossing edge gives a lighter tree
key_idea_summary: Let e be the lightest edge across the cut and T a spanning tree not containing e. Adding e to T creates a cycle, which must cross the cut an even number of times, so it contains another crossing edge f with weight greater than e. Then T + e - f is a spanning tree lighter than T. Hence no tree without e is minimal, and the minimum spanning tree contains e.
additional_sources: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein - Introduction to Algorithms

title: The Three Squares Problem: arctan 1 + arctan 1/2 + arctan 1/3 = 90 Degrees

key_idea_summary: The three angles are the arguments of 1 + i, 2 + i and 3 + i. Multiplying, (1 + i)(2 + i) = 1 + 3i and (1 + 3i)(3 + i) = 10i, a positive multiple of i, whose argument is pi/2. Since arguments add under multiplication and each angle is less than pi/2, the sum is exactly pi/2.

title: Turning Turtles Is Nim in Disguise
answer: Read each O in position k as a Nim heap of size k; the position is a loss for the player to move exactly when the XOR of the positions of the O's is 0.
key_idea: an O at position k is a Nim heap of size k
key_idea_summary: Turning the O at position k to X removes a heap of size k; turning it and flipping position j < k to O replaces heap k by heap j (and two equal heaps cancel in Nim, which handles the case where j already had an O). So the game is exactly Nim, solved by the XOR rule.
additional_sources: Berlekamp, Conway, Guy - Winning Ways for Your Mathematical Plays

title: The Two Envelopes Paradox: No Uniform Prior on All Amounts
answer: the assumption that 'the other is 2A or A/2 with probability 1/2 each' for every A cannot hold: it would require a uniform prior on all amounts, which does not exist
key_idea: write the two amounts as x and 2x; conditional on seeing A, the probability that A is the smaller amount depends on the prior distribution of x and cannot be 1/2 for all A
key_idea_summary: Model the envelopes as x and 2x with x drawn from some prior. Seeing A, the odds that the other holds 2A rather than A/2 are P(x = A) : P(x = A/2), which depends on the prior. If they were 1 : 1 for every A, the prior would give equal weight to A, 2A, 4A, ..., which no probability distribution can do. Unconditionally, switching gains or loses x with equal probability: expected gain zero.

title: The Monk Climbing the Mountain
key_idea: superimpose the two days: two monks on the same day must meet
key_idea_summary: Run both journeys on the same day: one monk ascending, another descending, both from dawn to sunset. They are on the same path going in opposite directions, so at some moment they are at the same point.
additional_sources: Gardner - The Colossal Book of Short Puzzles and Problems
aliases: mountain climbing problem (same time both days)

title: The Fly Between Two Trains
key_idea: ignore the zigzags: the fly flies for exactly as long as the trains take to meet
key_idea_summary: The trains close their 100 km gap at 100 km/h, meeting after 1 hour. The fly flies at 75 km/h for that whole hour, so it covers 75 km, regardless of how many times it turns.
additional_sources: Gardner - The Colossal Book of Short Puzzles and Problems

title: Varignon's Theorem: the Midpoints of Any Quadrilateral Form a Parallelogram
key_idea: with position vectors, the midpoint of AB is (a + b)/2, and consecutive midpoints differ by half a diagonal
key_idea_summary: Let the vertices be a, b, c, d. The midpoints are (a+b)/2, (b+c)/2, (c+d)/2, (d+a)/2. Consecutive differences are (c - a)/2, (d - b)/2, (a - c)/2, (b - d)/2: opposite sides are equal and parallel, both parallel to a diagonal. The parallelogram's sides are half the diagonals, and its area is half the quadrilateral's.

title: Wolf, Goat and Cabbage as a Path in a State Graph
answer: take the goat over, return, take the wolf (or cabbage) over, bring the goat back, take the cabbage (or wolf) over, return, take the goat over; seven crossings
key_idea: draw the graph whose vertices are the safe configurations and whose edges are single crossings; the solution is a path
key_idea_summary: A configuration records which of the four (farmer, wolf, goat, cabbage) are on the far bank; only 10 of the 16 are safe. Joining configurations that differ by one legal crossing gives a small graph in which the start and goal are connected by exactly two shortest paths of length 7, both starting and ending with the goat.

title: Wythoff's Nim and the Golden Ratio
answer: the pairs (floor(k phi), floor(k phi^2)) for k = 0, 1, 2, ..., where phi is the golden ratio: (0,0), (1,2), (3,5), (4,7), (6,10), ...
key_idea: the losing positions are generated greedily (each uses the smallest unused first coordinate, with difference k), and the two coordinate sequences are complementary Beatty sequences, which forces the golden ratio
key_idea_summary: Losing positions (a_k, b_k) have distinct first coordinates, distinct second coordinates and distinct differences, and every integer occurs as a coordinate; so they are generated greedily with b_k = a_k + k. Two complementary sequences floor(k alpha), floor(k beta) require 1/alpha + 1/beta = 1 (Beatty), and beta = alpha + 1 forces alpha = phi.
additional_sources: Berlekamp, Conway, Guy - Winning Ways for Your Mathematical Plays

title: The Coins-in-a-Row Game: Take All the Odd Positions or All the Even Ones
answer: colour the positions alternately; the first player can take all coins of whichever colour class has the larger total
key_idea: the first player can always take a coin of a chosen parity class, and can force the second player to expose only coins of the other class
key_idea_summary: Number the positions 1..2n. The end coins are positions 1 and 2n, one odd and one even. If the first player takes an odd-position coin, the exposed ends are both even; whatever the second player takes, the new end is again odd, and the first player takes it. So the first player collects exactly the odd positions (or, symmetrically, the even ones) and picks the class with the larger sum.
additional_sources: Winkler - Mathematical Puzzles, A Connoisseur's Collection
aliases: first player never loses the coin game

title: Coins on a Round Table
key_idea: take the centre, then mirror every move through the centre
key_idea_summary: The first player places a coin at the centre and afterwards answers each opponent move with its point reflection through the centre. The reflected spot is always free (its mirror image was free before the opponent's move and does not overlap the central coin), so the first player always has a move.
source_name: Fomin, Genkin, Itenberg - Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience)

title: The Arithmetic and Harmonic Means of the Divisors Multiply to n
key_idea: the map d -> n/d permutes the divisors, so the sum of 1/d equals (1/n) times the sum of d
key_idea_summary: Since d -> n/d is a bijection of the divisor set, sum over d of 1/d = sum over d of 1/(n/d) = (1/n) sum over d of d. With k divisors, H(n) = k/(sum 1/d) = kn/(sum d) = n/A(n).

title: The Divisor-Naming Game: Pair d with n/d
answer: the second player, by answering every divisor d with its partner under the pairing {1, 10}, {2, 50}, {4, 25}, {5, 20}
key_idea: the eight safe divisors pair up so that the second player can always answer with the partner of the first player's move, and the player naming the eighth safe divisor forces the other to say 100
key_idea_summary: The safe divisors are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50, eight in all, so the second player names the last safe one and the first player is then forced to name 100. To guarantee this the second player answers each move by its partner in the pairing {1, 10}, {2, 50}, {4, 25}, {5, 20}: the partner is always still available, so the second player always has a safe move.
source_name: Fomin, Genkin, Itenberg - Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience)

title: A Number Has an Odd Number of Divisors Iff It Is a Perfect Square
key_idea: pair each divisor d with n/d; the pairing is an involution whose only possible fixed point is sqrt(n)
key_idea_summary: The map d -> n/d pairs the divisors of n. A divisor is paired with itself only when d = n/d, i.e. d^2 = n. So the divisors come in pairs, plus one unpaired divisor exactly when n is a square.

title: Placing Dominoes on an Even Board: the Second Player Mirrors
answer: the second player, by placing each domino in the position centrally symmetric to the first player's last domino
key_idea: central symmetry of the even board pairs up every domino position with a disjoint partner
key_idea_summary: Rotate the board by 180 degrees about its centre. Every domino position is mapped to another domino position, disjoint from the original because the centre of the board is a corner point, not a cell (the board has even sides). The second player always has the mirror move available: if the mirror position overlapped an earlier domino, the original would have overlapped that domino's mirror image, already present.
additional_sources: Berlekamp, Conway, Guy - Winning Ways for Your Mathematical Plays
aliases: domino placement game second player wins

title: The Expected Maximum of n Uniform Random Numbers Is n/(n + 1)
key_idea: the n points cut [0, 1] into n + 1 gaps that are exchangeable, so each gap has expected length 1/(n + 1)
key_idea_summary: The n points divide [0, 1] into n + 1 gaps whose joint distribution is symmetric under permuting the gaps (by the symmetry of the uniform distribution). Since the gaps sum to 1, each has expected length 1/(n + 1). The maximum is 1 minus the last gap, so its expectation is 1 - 1/(n + 1) = n/(n + 1).
additional_sources: Feller - An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, vol. 2

title: Expected Position of the First Ace by Symmetry
answer: 10.6 (the first ace is at position 53/5 = 10.6 on average)
key_idea: the four aces divide the 48 other cards into five gaps that are exchangeable, so each gap has expected size 48/5
key_idea_summary: The 48 non-aces fall into five gaps: before the first ace, between consecutive aces, and after the last. By symmetry of the random shuffle the five gaps have the same distribution, and they sum to 48, so each has mean 48/5 = 9.6. The first ace is at position 9.6 + 1 = 10.6.
additional_sources: Mosteller - Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability
aliases: first ace in a shuffled deck
expected number of cards before the first ace

title: Gauss's Pairing for 1 + 2 + ... + n
key_idea: add the sum to its reversal
key_idea_summary: Write the sum forwards and backwards and add column-wise: every column is 1 + n, 2 + (n-1), ..., all equal to n + 1. Two copies of the sum therefore equal n(n+1).
aliases: sum of the first n integers
write the sum forwards and backwards

title: The Hundred Lockers Puzzle
key_idea: locker n is toggled once per divisor of n, and only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors
key_idea_summary: Locker n is toggled by student k exactly when k divides n, so it is toggled d(n) times and ends open iff d(n) is odd. Divisors pair off as d and n/d, so d(n) is odd only when n is a square (when sqrt(n) pairs with itself).
additional_sources: Gardner - The Colossal Book of Short Puzzles and Problems

title: I Cut, You Choose: a Fair Division by Symmetry
answer: the cutter cuts into two pieces of equal value in her own eyes; the chooser takes the piece he values more
key_idea: the cutter neutralises the chooser's freedom by making the choice irrelevant to her, and the chooser's freedom guarantees him the better half
key_idea_summary: The cutter divides the cake into two pieces she values equally, so whichever piece is taken she keeps exactly half of her value. The chooser takes the piece he values at least as much as the other; since the two pieces together are the whole cake, that piece is worth at least half to him.

title: An Integral Evaluated by Reflection
key_idea: the substitution x -> pi/2 - x swaps sin and cos, so the integral equals its partner with cos on top; the two add to the integral of 1
key_idea_summary: Let I be the integral and J the same with cos x in the numerator. The substitution x -> pi/2 - x turns I into J, so I = J. But I + J is the integral of 1 over [0, pi/2], which is pi/2. Hence I = pi/4.
aliases: integral of sin/(sin+cos) from 0 to pi/2

title: Base Angles of an Isosceles Triangle Are Equal (Pappus's Proof)
key_idea: the triangle is congruent to its own mirror image: compare triangle ABC with triangle ACB
key_idea_summary: Triangles ABC and ACB (the same triangle with B and C swapped) have AB = AC, AC = AB and the included angle at A in common, so they are congruent by SAS. Corresponding angles are equal: angle B of the first corresponds to angle C of the second.
aliases: Pappus's proof by congruence with the mirror image

title: Kayles on a Row: the First Player Wins by Symmetry
answer: the first player knocks down the middle pin (n odd) or the middle two pins (n even), then mirrors every move of the opponent in the other half
key_idea: remove the centre so that the remaining pins form two identical rows, then copy the opponent's moves symmetrically
key_idea_summary: After the first move the row is split into two equal, non-interacting rows. Whatever the second player does in one row, the first player does the mirror image in the other row. The first player always has a reply, so the second player runs out of moves first.
additional_sources: Berlekamp, Conway, Guy - Winning Ways for Your Mathematical Plays
aliases: knock down one or two adjacent pins

title: Two Guards, One Question: Compose a Truth-Teller with a Liar
answer: ask either guard 'If I asked the other guard whether this door leads to freedom, would he say yes?' and take the opposite of the answer
key_idea: routing the question through both guards composes one truth and one lie, so the answer is always the negation of the truth, regardless of whom you ask
key_idea_summary: Whichever guard you ask, the hypothetical answer passes through one liar and one truth-teller: the truth-teller reports the liar's lie, and the liar misreports the truth-teller's truth. Either way the reply is the negation of the truth, so the opposite of the reply is reliable.
additional_sources: Smullyan - What Is the Name of This Book?
aliases: what would the other guard say

title: A Number n Has at Most 2 sqrt(n) Divisors
key_idea: pair each divisor d with n/d; in each pair one member is at most sqrt(n)
key_idea_summary: The involution d -> n/d pairs the divisors, and in every pair {d, n/d} the smaller one is at most sqrt(n). So the divisors are determined by their small members, of which there are at most sqrt(n); hence at most 2 sqrt(n) divisors in total.
aliases: divisors pair up around sqrt n

title: Losing Positions of the Scoring Game Are Multiples of k + 1
answer: normal play: multiples of k + 1 lose; misere play: positions n with n = 1 mod (k + 1) lose
key_idea: the complement pairing m -> k + 1 - m works in both versions, shifted by one in the misere case
key_idea_summary: Normal play: from a multiple of k + 1 every move leaves a non-multiple, and from a non-multiple one can move to a multiple, so multiples of k + 1 lose. Misere play: taking the last counter loses, so leaving exactly 1 counter is the goal; the same pairing shows that positions n = 1 mod (k + 1) lose.
aliases: single pile take up to k

title: Penney's Game: Always Pick the Pattern That Beats the Opponent's
answer: if the first player picks XYZ, the second picks (not Y) X Y; this wins with probability at least 2/3 in every case
key_idea: the second player's pattern ends with the first two symbols of the opponent's pattern, so whenever the opponent's pattern is about to complete, the second player's has usually just completed
key_idea_summary: Against XYZ choose WXY with W = not Y. Whenever XYZ is about to complete, the toss before its X was either W, in which case WXY already occurred and the second player has won, or Y, which is rarer. A short Markov-chain computation gives the second player's winning probability as 2/3 or 3/4 for the six mixed patterns and 7/8 against HHH or TTT. Every pattern is beaten by some other pattern: the relation is non-transitive.
additional_sources: Gardner - Time Travel and Other Mathematical Bewilderments

title: Six Successive Point Reflections Return Every Point
key_idea: the composition of two point reflections is a translation, so three of them make a point reflection, which is an involution
key_idea_summary: Reflecting through A then B sends P to P + 2(B - A), a translation. Hence reflecting through A, B, C in turn is a translation followed by a point reflection, itself a point reflection (through A - B + C). Applying a point reflection twice is the identity.
aliases: reflect in A then B then C

title: Proizvolov's Identity
key_idea: in every pair (a_i, b_i) exactly one number is at most n and the other exceeds n
key_idea_summary: Claim: for each i, one of a_i, b_i is in {1..n} and the other in {n+1..2n}. Then |a_i - b_i| = (large one) - (small one), and summing over i, the large ones are exactly n+1, ..., 2n and the small ones exactly 1, ..., n, so the sum is (n+1 + ... + 2n) - (1 + ... + n) = n^2.

title: On a Cycle, the Last New Vertex Visited by a Random Walk Is Uniform
answer: each of the n - 1 other vertices is last with probability 1/(n - 1)
key_idea: to be the last vertex, v must be reached only after the walk has covered everything else, which happens exactly when the walk, starting next to v, reaches the far side of v before v; by symmetry this probability does not depend on v
key_idea_summary: Fix a vertex v != 0 with neighbours u and w. Vertex v is visited last iff, from the first moment the walk hits u or w (say u), it reaches w by going the long way around before stepping onto v. This is the gambler's-ruin probability of reaching a point at distance n - 1 before a point at distance 1 on a line, namely 1/(n - 1), independent of v.
additional_sources: Lovasz - Random walks on graphs: a survey
aliases: last vertex visited on a cycle

title: Two Reflections in Parallel Lines Make a Translation
key_idea: track the signed distance to the lines: each reflection negates it relative to its own line, and two negations compose to a shift
key_idea_summary: Use a coordinate x perpendicular to the lines, with l at x = 0 and m at x = d. Reflection in l sends x to -x and reflection in m sends x to 2d - x, so together they send x to x + 2d: a translation by 2d. For lines meeting at angle t, the same bookkeeping on the polar angle gives a -> a + 2t, a rotation by 2t.

title: The Vertex Vectors of a Regular Polygon Sum to Zero
key_idea: the sum is invariant under a rotation that moves every non-zero vector
key_idea_summary: Rotating the plane by 2 pi/n permutes the vertices, so it maps the sum vector to itself. The only vector fixed by a rotation through an angle that is not a multiple of 2 pi is the zero vector.
aliases: sum of roots of unity is zero

title: The Subtraction Game (Take 1 to k): Complement to k + 1
answer: The player to move loses if and only if n is a multiple of k + 1; otherwise they win by moving to a multiple of k + 1 and thereafter answering each removal of m with a removal of k + 1 - m.
key_idea: pair the moves so that each round removes exactly k + 1 counters
key_idea_summary: Whatever m in 1..k the opponent takes, reply with k + 1 - m, which is also in 1..k. Each pair of moves removes exactly k + 1 counters, so from a multiple of k + 1 the replying player always faces a multiple of k + 1 and eventually takes the last counter.
additional_sources: Fomin, Genkin, Itenberg - Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience)
aliases: nim with one heap and a maximum take

title: At Most 32 Non-Attacking Knights on a Chessboard
key_idea: pair the 64 squares into 32 pairs joined by a knight's move; each pair holds at most one knight
key_idea_summary: Every knight move joins squares of opposite colour, so 32 knights on the white squares never attack each other. For the upper bound, partition the board into 32 pairs of squares a knight's move apart (a closed knight's tour gives such a pairing by taking alternate edges). Two knights in the same pair would attack each other, so at most one knight per pair: at most 32.
aliases: pair the squares by knight moves

title: Three Random Points on a Circle Lie in a Semicircle with Probability 3/4
answer: 3/4 for lying in a semicircle, hence 3/4 for an obtuse triangle (the inscribed triangle is obtuse iff the points lie in a semicircle)
key_idea: the events 'the semicircle starting at point i (going clockwise) contains the other two' are disjoint and each has probability 1/4
key_idea_summary: If the three points lie in a semicircle, exactly one of them is the 'first' point of that semicircle in the clockwise direction. For a fixed point, the other two lie in the clockwise semicircle starting there with probability (1/2)^2 = 1/4. The three events are disjoint, so the probability is 3 * 1/4 = 3/4. An inscribed triangle is obtuse iff its vertices lie in a semicircle (Thales), so the obtuse probability is also 3/4.
additional_sources: Mosteller - Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability
aliases: random triangle is obtuse with probability 3/4

title: Extracting a Fair Coin from a Biased One (von Neumann)
answer: toss twice; HT means 'heads', TH means 'tails', and HH or TT means toss again
key_idea: the outcomes HT and TH have the same probability p(1 - p) by symmetry, whatever p is
key_idea_summary: Two independent tosses give HT with probability p(1 - p) and TH with probability (1 - p)p, equal for every p. Discarding HH and TT and repeating, the first decisive pair is HT or TH with equal conditional probability 1/2.
additional_sources: von Neumann - Various techniques used in connection with random digits
aliases: fair bit from a biased coin

title: Wilson's Theorem by Pairing Each Residue with Its Inverse
key_idea: pair each residue with its multiplicative inverse; only 1 and -1 are self-paired
key_idea_summary: Modulo a prime every nonzero residue x has a unique inverse, and x is its own inverse only if x^2 = 1, i.e. x = 1 or x = -1. So in the product 1 * 2 * ... * (p-1) all other factors cancel in inverse pairs, leaving 1 * (-1) = -1.
additional_sources: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK

title: Zagier's One-Sentence Proof That Primes 1 mod 4 Are Sums of Two Squares
key_idea: two involutions on the same finite set, one of which has exactly one fixed point
key_idea_summary: Let S be the finite set of triples (x, y, z) of positive integers with x^2 + 4yz = p. Zagier's piecewise-linear involution on S has exactly one fixed point, so |S| is odd. The simple involution (x, y, z) -> (x, z, y) therefore also has a fixed point, i.e. a triple with y = z, giving p = x^2 + (2y)^2.
source_name: Aigner & Ziegler - Proofs from THE BOOK
